supervision, nor has it the ability to take care of such a large number of 
monuments. I have seen every monumen t in India. The Raza Library at 
Rampur I can talk of. Will the Minister review this seriously and try to have a 
new worthwhile and extensive policy, including the role of private industry

*262. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have introduced any Night Shelter Scheme for 
the shelterless and pavement dwellers; 
(b) if so, when the scheme was introduced; and 
.   (c) the funds released so far, by Government for this scheme State and 
year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Night Shelter Scheme was introduced in 1988-89 to provide Night 
Shelter and Pay & Use toilet facilities to urban shelterless. 
The Scheme was modified in August 1992 to cover all urban centres 
having concentration of footpath dwe llers/homeless and renamed as "Shelter 
& Sanitation Facilities for footpath Dwellers in Urban Areas." Since October, 
2002, the scheme has been revised and renamed as "Night Shelter for Urban 
Shelterless." The scheme is now limited to construction of composite Night 
Shelters with community toilets and baths for urban shelterless. This is a 
demand driven scheme and its implementation is undertaken by the State 
Government or local municipal bodies  or State sponsored agencies and 
proposals are mooted by them. Under the scheme, Government of India 
subsidy of 50% of the cost of construction (subject to cost ceiling of Rs. 
20,000 per bed) is given to implementing agencies

Tribals residing in forests 
†*269. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that tribal people residing in forests remain naked 
even today; 
(b) if so, the number thereof; and 
(c) the details of Government's action plan to improve their standard of 
living? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH) (a) to 
(c) There are two Scheduled Tribes in  Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the 
Jarawas and Sentinelese who are residing  in forests and remain almost naked 
even today. The Jarawas and Sentineles e are declared as aboriginal tribes 
since 1956. They were along with other tribes declared Scheduled Tribes in 
1959. As per 2001 Census, the Jarawas are 240 and the Sentinelese are 39 in 
number estimated. The Sentinelese are still hostile and live in isolation in 
North Sentinel Island. The Andaman and Nicobar Administration provide gift 
etc. from a distance. Jarawas are living in South and Middle Andaman. 
Andaman and Nicobar Administration has informed that the population of 
Jarawas is now 266. Andaman and Nicobar Islands declared certain territories 
as reserve for aboriginal people of the Island and some parts of South and 
Middle Andaman were reserv ed for Jarawas. The Jarawas were hostile but 
have come in contact with outsiders si nce 1997. The contact of Jarawas with 
outsiders led to some problems such as measles, skin diseases etc. 
The Andaman and Nicobar Administration has taken action for the welfare 
of the Jarawas:— 
1. Exclusive natural resources base i.e. Jarawa tribal forest reserve has 
been increased from 847 sq. kms. to 1028 sq. kms. for their foraging. 
2. Exclusive marine resource base has also been increased by declaring 
coastal water up to 5 km. from high tide mark as tribal reserve. 
3. Jarawa tribal reseve has been carved out taking into account natural 
features like hill range peaks, creeks etc. as far as practicable so that 
boundaries of the reserve area is intelligible to all concerned

thereby trespass into reserve area is avoided. There will be no .        
intervention in the day to day life of the Jarawas. 
4. Andaman Trunk Road belt has been decreased from 200 meters on 
either side of the tar road to only 30 meters from the center line of 
the road on either side. 
5. Enforcement measures have been  intensified by the Police and 
Forest to protect the Jarawa resource base in the Forest and coastal 
water. 
6. Police, trained anthropologists and other welfare functionaries are 
pressed into service for regular patrolling at vulnerable places to 
prevent unauthorized contact of non-tribals with the Jarawas. 
7. Sites of Police, Forest and PWD are reviewed and rationalized by 
relocating some of them as far away  as possible from the vicinity of 
Jarawas territory to avoid non-Jarawa's proximity to Jarawas. 
8. Standing Health Team consisting of experience and selected doctors 
has been constituted which visits the Jarawas in the forest 
periodically to make assessment of their health and provide required 
care in the Jarawa area itself to the extent feasible. 
9. Trained health workers are deployed in the field daily to provide 
treatment for minor ailments in situ and thereby avoiding evacuation 
of Jarawas to the hospital for minor ailment. 
 
10. Jarawa patients are shifted to hospital only when it is inevitable 
keeping in view their health interest/to save their life. 
11. Separate/exclusive hospital wards for Jarawas have been provided 
and such wards are declared as Trib al Reserve, the entry into which 
by non-tribals is prohibited without the permit from the competent 
authority.

*275. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state:

judicial accountability as per the resolution passed by the Apex Court;

(c) if so, whether any steps are being considered to stop the erosion of 
people's trust; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H,R. BHARDWAJ) (a) 
to (d) Attention of the Government has been drawn, from time to time, to the 
question of enforcing judicial accountability. 
2. The issue was discussed at the Conference of Chief Justices held in 
1990 and on the basis of the broad consensus emerging out of the 
deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice of the High Co urt has the competence to receive 
complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when he 
receives any, he would look into it for fi nding out if it deserves to be closely 
looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires to be examined, he 
shall have facts ascertained in such  manner as he considers appropriate 
keeping the nature of allegations in view and if he is of the opinion that the 
matter is such that it should be reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall 
do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to 
complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and in regard 
to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. On the basis of the facts 
ascertained, the Chief Justice of the High  Court or the Supr eme Court, as the 
case may be, shall take such appropriat e action as may be considered proper, 
keeping the interests of the judiciary as the paramount consideration." 
3. The complaints received against the Judges of the Supreme Court 
and the High Courts are dealt with in the manner indicated above. The 
Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 specifies the procedure to deal with misconduct/

misdemeanour of Judges of the Supreme Court/High Courts, but Government 
has no constitutional competence to order enquiry against them.

Report on ICHR 
*278. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received an interim report of the one-man 
Review Committee of the Indian Council for Historical Research (ICHR); 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH) (a) to (c) The one-man  Review Committee enquiring into 
the affairs of the Indian Council of Hi storical Research (ICHR) has so far 
submitted two interim reports. These relate to the "non-publication/stoppage 
of volumes of Towards Freedom' Project by ICHR"; and, on the "non-
submission of research work by scholars, who were given Fellowships by the 
ICHR during the period between 1995-96 and 2000-01, as highlighted in the 
report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for 2002-03". 
42 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In its interim report on the 'Towards Freedom' Project, the Committee has 
observed that attempts were made to scuttle the project through stoppage of 
funds and interruption in the publication of the volumes. The Committee has 
recommended the completion of the project within 24 months and the 
constitution of an Editorial Board with an eminent historian as the General 
Editor. The Committee has also recommended the streamlining of the 
procedures of publication and has suggested that the Government take a view 
regarding the present Council, including its Chairman. 
On the issue of the 'non-submission of research work by scholars', the 
Committee has observed irregularities in the award of the Senior Research 
Fellowships and the National Fellowships, such as no proper representation 
to the different regions of the count ry, SCs/STs, women and the minorities. 
The Committee has recommended a St anding Search Committee to award 
National Fellowships, and the institution of a system of nominations to the 
Senior Search Fellowships as well as the computerisation of the fellowships 
programme and, the travel grant programme. The Committee has also 
recommended the recovery of fellowship grants from the defaulters. 
The Government has accepted the re commendations of the Committee in 
the interim report on the "non-publication/stoppage of volumes of Towards 
Freedom Project", and the ICHR has been directed to take action on the 
same. The interim report of the Committee on "non-submission of research 
work by scholars" is under examination.

*279. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether UNESCO has made concrete suggestions for upkeep of Taj 
Mahal at Agra and maintenance of its surroundings and environment;

THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY) (a) Yes Sir. 
Based on the UNESCO-ICOMOS Joint Monitoring Mission, the UNESCO 
World Heritage Committee in its meeting held in June-July 2004 has made 
the following recommendations concerning the World Heritage properties 
Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri. 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2005] 
(i)  Set up a body to coordinate and address all the conservation and 
development challenges of the three World Heritage properties in 
the Agra District by involving all the stakeholders. 
(ii) Evaluate and redefine the World Heritage protective boundaries and 
management guidelines pertaining to the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort. 
(iii)  Integrate the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort as one protected World 
Heritage area to ensure better ma nagement of the property, with a 
possible inclusion of Fatehpur Sikri subject to a broader regional 
planning scheme. 
(iv)   Elaborate a comprehensive site management plan, including a 
specific visitor management plan, based on a regional plan for 
conservation and development of the World Heritage properties, and 
ensure its implementation. 
(v) Improve the on-site interpretation and visitor management at the 
World Heritage properties. 
(vi) Set up on-site monitoring mechanisms, to assess the impact of urban 
development on the World Heritage values of the properties and 
their surrounding areas so as to integrate the protection of urban 
landscape into the overall heritage protection mechanism. 
(vii) Organise a National Workshop on the elaboration of Site 
Management Plans for the preparation of the World Heritage 
extension(s), including the upgrading of the protective boundary and 
buffer zones. 
(c) Steps are being taken for preparation of comprehensive site 
management plan for all the three World Heritage Sites.

Saffronisation of school syllabus 
2038. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of controversy regarding saffronisation of school syllabus 
during the last regime; 
(b) whether it has affected the curriculum in any manners; and 
(c) if so, in what manner Government would rectify the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The 
National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCFSE) was brought 
out by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
in the year 2000. The textbooks developed by NCERT under the NCFSE-
2000 engaged public and academic attention on account of several 
inadequacies. A panel of three eminent historians was constituted by the 
Government to conduct a review of NCERT history textbooks because of 
reported biases and inadequacies th erein. The Executiv e Committee of the 
NCERT in July, 2004 considered the Report of the panel. In view of the 
advanced stage of the current academ ic session, it was decided that the 
existing NCERT history textbooks, excluding the controversial portions, 
would be used by the students of the CBSE affiliated schools alongwith the 
advisory prepared by NCERT. Five copies each of the history textbooks used 
in the CBSE schools prior to the introduction of the controversial history 
textbooks were also distributed free of cost to all the schools for teachers for 
use as reference books. 
To comply with the decision of th e Executive Body for restoring the 
NCERT textbooks after effecting approp riate modifications in line with the 
existing curriculum for the academic  session 2005-06, the following 
Committees were constituted by the NCERT:— 
74 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) A History Committee was constituted for making necessary 
recommendations to review pre-2000 NCERT histroy textbooks. The old 
NCERT history textbooks, after incorporation of necessary changes based on 
the recommendations of this Committee, would be restored during 2005-06. 
(b) In respect of textbooks other than history textbooks, Quick Review 
Committees were also constituted by NCERT and errors pointed out by these 
Committees have been incorporated as errata in the NCERT textbooks for the 
next academic year. 
In keeping with the 5-yearly mandate of the National Policy on Education 
(NPE) as well as the decision of the Executive Committee of NCERT, a 
review of the NCFSE has been initiated by the NCERT in the current 
academic year. For this purpose, a National Steering Group of eminent 
scholars, activists and teachers has been constituted by the NCERT. In 
addition, 21 National Focus Groups covering different subject areas, issues of 
structural reorganization of the education, those of national concern such as 
gender, problems of the SC/ST children, etc. have also been constituted. 
The Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) has separately set up a 
committee on 10.9.2004, inter alia, to suggest an appr opriate regulatory 
mechanism for institutionalizing the issu e of preparation of textbooks and 
curricular material. 
The recommendations of the National Steering Group/Focus Groups and 
those of the Committee set up by CABE would be important inputs in a 
revised NCFSE.

2046. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that more than 10 per cent girls in the country get 
married before attaining the age of 14, according to studies conducted by 
Population Council of India; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to impose ban on such underage 
marriages by educating the parents through Government agencies/NGOs?

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH) (a) Yes, Sir. 
As per the report of International Institute for Population Sciences, the 
percentage of currently married women in the age group of 25-29 got married 
by the age of 13 years is 12.1 and th at the percentage of women in the age 
group of 20-24 has been dropped to 8.9 and in the age group of 15-19 to 4.7. 
(b) The Government is taking all necessary steps to reduce the child 
marriages. 
83

from the country. Such as, 
* State Governments have been asked for strict implementation of Child 
Marriage (Restraint) Act, 1929; 
* State Governments have been asked to take necessary measures to 
prevdnt child marriages in their States; 
* The proposal for amendment to the Child Marriage (Restraint) Act, 
1929 is presently under consideration of a Parliamentary Standing 
Committee which would help in better implementation of the Act;

* A strong media campaign is being launched by the Department of 
Women and Child Development especi ally to target prevention of 
child marriages in the forthcoming festival season of Akshaya Teej;

Examination stress 
2050. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR : Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the examination stress continues to take a heavy toll of life of 
students, year after year, despite implementation of the recommendations of 
the Examination Reforms Commission; 
(b) if so, the number of suicides committed by students in Delhi and other 
States so far during the examinations this year and the comparative figures 
for the last three years; and 
(c) the steps taken/being taken to ease such stress further? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI) (a) Yes, Sir. 
However, it is not only examination stress but various other contributory 
factors such as parental pressure increasing competition and fast changing 
social and economic conditions wh ich at times compel students to 
depression. 
(b) There are three suicide reports pub lished in the newspapers wherein 
examination stress has been stated to be the cause of suicide by the students. 
(c) The steps taken to reduce stress among students are as follows: 
(i) Launching of 'helpline' one month before the commencement of 
examination also before the declaration of results. 
(ii) Publication of sample question papers and marking schemes to 
familiarize students and teachers about the nature of questions and 
question papers 
(iii) Elimination of ov erall aggregation of marks to reduce unhealthy 
competition among students. 
(iv) Introduction of comprehensive and continuous school based 
evaluation. 
(v) Providing facility of compartment examination in two subjects in 
class X and one subject in class XII. 
(vi) Providing three chances of co mpartment examination for class X 
and XII.

to provide more internal choices of questions.

group of women in difficult circumstances through a home-based holistic and 
integrated approach.

Pirated CDs and DVDs 
2093. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that pirated CDs and DVDs are easily accessible in 
the open market which are ruining the music and film industry; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to check this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) According to Federation of lndian Chamber 
of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) the revenue loss from film piracy is about 
Rs. 1200 crores annually. As far as Musi c Industry is concerned, the Indian 
Music Industry (IMI) has informed that  the size of the music industry has 
fallen from Rs. 1000 crores in 1999 to Rs.500 crores in 2004 due to piracy. 
The Ministry does not have any data. 
(c)The Copyright Act, 1957, which falis under the purview of the Ministry 
of Human Resource Development contains, inter alia the legal provisions 
regarding copyright in cinematograph films and music. The responsibility for 
dealing with offences under the Copyright Act rests with the police 
authorities of the State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. 
Copyright Enforcement cells have been set up in most States/UT 
Administrations headed by a senior police officer to deal with such offences. 
Apart from this, the Ministry of Information and Broadcastiang has taken 
the following steps to fight piracy in the film sector; 
• This Ministry has a Plan Scheme  to undertake activities relating to 
anti piracy measures. The Ministry has initiated action to formulate 
appropriate training modules for po lice officers to train them for 
anti-piracy. 
• In September 2001, Ministry of l&B brought together 
representatives of the film produ cers, multi-service operators and 
cable operators who have jointly resolved not to exhibit films 
without valid permission from the copyright holders. 
• Recognizing that high levels of entertainment tax lead to piracy, the 
Committee for Development of th e Entertainment Sector, a sub 
committee of the State Information Ministers' Conference, 
122 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA  SABHA 
recommended that the rate of entertainment tax be lowered to a 
ceiling of 45%. A number of States have suitably lowered their 
entertainment tax levels. 
• The Committee also recommended appointment of senior police 
officers in States to work in co -ordination with the entertainment 
industry, as nodal officers. 
• During the Budget of 2003-04, audio CDs were exempted from 
excise duty to do away with the pr ice advantage available to pirated 
CDs. 
• The Public Service Broadcasting Trust has been entrusted with the 
task of making a film on piracy. 
• The Cable Television Networks Regulation Act has been amended 
in 2000, to prohibit a Cable operator from transmitting or re-
transmitting any programme or channel for which the Copyright 
holder has not granted him a license. 
• This Ministry has requested Chief Secretaries of all States to advise 
District Magistrates and Superintendents of Police to include anti 
piracy measures in their monthly activity reports.

DASARI NARAYANA RAO); (a) No, Sir. Section 1-8 of the Mines and 
Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) enjoins

which the applicant proposes to make in the mines and in the industry based 
on the minerals while deciding merits of various applicants.

Problems of Jhuggis 
†2152. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any scheme to tackle the 
problem of increasing Jhuggies in the cities; and 
(b) the population inhabited in Jhuggies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
Slum development is a State subject . The State Governments formulate 
specific plans, programmes and schemes for development of slums in various 
towns/cities as per their priorities and ma ke necessary provisions therefor in 
their respective State Plans. However, with a view to ameliorate the living 
conditions of the slum dwellers, a programme known as National Slum 
Development Programme (NSDP) was launched at the national level by the 
Government in August, 1996 for the development of urban slums. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2005] 
Besides, a Centrally sponsored Scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas 
Yojana (VAMBAY) was launched on 2.12.2001 with a view to ameliorating 
the conditions of the urban slum dwellers living below the poverty line who 
do not possess adequate shelter. The Scheme has the primary objective to 
facilitate the construction and upgradation of the dwelling units for the slum 
dwellers and to provide health and enabling urban environment through 
community toilets under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, a component of the 
Scheme. 
(b) Slum Development being a State subject, State Governments survey 
and take stock of slums/jhuggies in their respective States. However, the 
Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) conducted a one time 
study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report titled "a Compendium on 
India Slums-1996". According to this report the slum population of India is 
estimated to be 6.18 crores in 2001. 
An attempt was made for the first time during the Census of India, 2001 by 
the Registrar General of India to collect detailed data about slum population 
of the country but only in the cities/towns having 50.000 population or more 
based on 1991 census. As per the provisional figures of Census of India 2001, 
the slum population of such 607 towns/ cities of the country is 4.03 crores 
approximately.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, it is shocking to know that 
close to one in every three babies, that die before they are four week's old in 
the world, die in India. Of the 26 milli on children born in India each year, 1.2 
million die in the first four weeks and 30  per cent of the world's 3.9 million 
neonatal deaths take place in India. Th is has been revealed recently by the 
State of India's Newborns Report. The current Neonatal Mortality Rate is

lakh maternal deaths globally, each ye ar, are in India. So, I urge upon the 
Government of India to immediately ta ke measures to reduce the Neonatal 
Mortality Rate in India by taking necessary measures.

Demand for implementation of integrated drinking water scheme 
at Hogenakal, Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri are the 
most backward districts in Tamil Nadu. There is no adequate drinking water 
facility. The ground water level has gone down considerably. Even the little 
water available is not potable. A high content of fluoride is present which will 
endanger the lives of human beings and cattle. 
Due to concerted efforts of our Chief Minister, the rain water harvesting 
has been undertaken. But there is no respite from drinking water shortage. 
There is a waterfall in Hogenakal in Dharmapuri district. It is an important 
204 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
tourist centre. The water falling in the falls can be exploited for drinking water. 
The integrated drinking water scheme at Hogenakal, which would entail 
considerable expenditure, will solve the drinking water problem of Dharmapuri 
and Krishnagiri districts. Since the State was reeling under drought and recent 
tsunami disaster, the State is not in a position to invest the money. But the 
State is taking all steps to implement the project. 
Only with the assistance of Central Government, the project can be 
implemented. Although the matter was raised in Parliament several times by 
me, yet no action has been taken by the Central Government. 
There are no major industries in the Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri districts 
and, as such, there are no employment op portunities. Agriculture is the main 
occupation there. Since there is no water, agricultural operations have been 
affected. People may be forced to migrate to other places. 
It is estimated that about Rs. 1300 crore will be involved in the 
implementation of this project. I urge upon the Central Government to fully 
assist the State Government in this regard or obtain the World Bank loan at 
the earliest. Thank you, Sir.

That this House approves the Procla mation issued by the President on the

Before I explain the circumstances in which the Government has had to 
bring this Resolution to this august House, may I state that the Constitution 
framers had recognized that the provisi ons of article 356, among others, were 
necessary to meet the exceptional si tuation where the break down of the 
constitutional machinery occurs in a State. 
Now, may I take this opportunity to narrate briefly the circumstances 
prevailing in Bihar which led to the imposition of President's rule in the State. 
Elections to the Legislative Assembly of Bihar were held on 3rd, 15th and 
23rd of February, 2005. The number of s eats won by different political parties 
in the State, as emerged after c ounting on 27th February, 2005 are as 
follows:—

Smt. Rabri Devi tendered her resignation as Chief Minister on 28th 
February, 2005. She was asked to contin ue by the Governor till alternative 
arrangements were made. The Governor of Bi har kept a watch on the 
political situation. He assessed the claims made for formation of a popular 
206 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Government by two major coalitions and finally sent a report to the President 
on 6th March, 2005. As per the Govern or's report, the RJD and its alliance 
had the support of 92 MLAs, whereas the NDA alliance also had the support 
of 92 MLAs. 
A delegation of the members of UP met the Governor on 28th February, 
2005 and submitted a letter stating t ha they would neither support the RJD 
nor the BJP in the formation of the Go vernment in Bihar. In a subsequent 
meeting with the Governor, they reiterat ed their stand. The Governor, in his 
report already tabled in this august House, along with the President's 
Proclamation, gave a detailed account of his meetings with representatives of 
various political parties/alliances and some independent MLAs, and an 
analysis of how no combination of political parties or a coalition was able to 
form a Government, which would have the confidence of the majority of the 
members in the newly-constituted Assembly. 
Briefly, due to claims and counter-claims of various parties and alliances, 
without any supporting evidence, the Governor in his report stated that he had 
explored all the possibilities and he was fu lly satisfied that no political party or 
coalition of parties or groups was able to substantiate a claim of majority in 
the Legislative Assembly. According to the Governor, it was a case of 
complete inability of any political party to form a stable Government 
commanding the confidence of the majori ty of the Members. Therefore, the 
Governor recommended that the newly constituted Assembly be kept in 
suspended animation for the present and requested the President of India to 
take appropriate action, as required. 
The Budget of the State of Bihar for the year 2005-06 was yet to be 
passed. It would not have been appropriate for the caretaker Government to 
take any action regarding the passing of the Budget or a Vote-on-Account. 
There would have been serious financial and constitutional crises if the 
Budget or the Vote-on-Account were not passed before 31st March, 2005. 
The Union Cabinet, therefore, in its meeting held on 7th March, 2005 
considered the report of the Governor and the situation prevailing in Bihar, 
and decided to recommend to the President to issue a Proclamation under 
article 356 of the Constitution for imposing the President's rule in the State 
and keeping the State Legislative Assembly under suspended animation. 
On 7th March, 2005, the President was pleased to issue a Proclamation

under article 356(1) of the Constituti on imposing the President's rule in 
relation to the State of Bihar and keep ing the State Legislative Assembly 
under suspended animation. 
With these words, I commend, Sir, that the Proclamation issued on 7th 
March, 2005 under article 356 of the C onstitution in relation to the State of 
Bihar be approved by this august House. A copy of the Proclamation, as 
stipulated under the Constitution, along with consequential Order, is placed on 
the Table of the House. In keeping wi th the conventions, a copy of the 
Governor's report recommending issuance of the Proclamation is also placed 
on the Table of the House.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Excise Duty On Medicines 
*281. DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HE PTULLA: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to impose excise duty on 
medicines on maximum retail price instead of the price at which consumers 
buy medicines; 
(b) whether It is also a fact that duty has been hiked to 35 per cent to make it 
further difficult for the daily users to buy medicines; 
(c) what is the reason behind this sudden hike and how many medicines have 
been covered/spared by this hike; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement 
(a) With effect from 8.1.2005, the Government has prescribed levy of central 
excise duty on allopathic drugs on the basis of retail price, required to be declared 
under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995. 
(b) There has been no increase in the rate of excise duty on drugs and it 
continues to remain at 16 per cent ad-valorem. 
(c) and (d) The Government has prescribed levy of central excise duty on the 
basis of retail price to ensure certainty in assessment and avoid 

 
RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
valuation disputes for all allopathic medicines. Ayurvedic, Homoeopathic, Siddha, 
Unani and Biochemic drugs are outside the purview of retail price based levy. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: Hon. Chairman, Sir, already, the 
country is having a discussion about the patents. The Bill is going to come before 
this House and there would be a discusion on the rise in the prices of drugs, 
owing to a change from process patent to the product patent. I am sure the 
hon. Minister of Finance is aware of the steep price-rise which has taken place. Is 
the Government aware that the small scale units account for nearly half of the 
drug production in the country? This measure is going to hit the companies which 
have invested a lot of money with compliance to stringent manufacturing norms, 
and forces them to move out from Maharashtra, Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and 
West Bengal which are going to be very badly affected by it. And they will have to 
go to States like Himachal Pradesh, Uttaranchal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir 
which have got tax exemptions. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the hon. Member has raised several issues 
which are quite disparate issues. Now, what has been provided to Himachal 
Pradesh and Uttaranchal Pradesh are some tax exemptions, and this, the hon. 
Member will recall, was provided by the previous Government. Therefore, in 
respect of those tax exemptions, I can do nothing except that we have put a sunset 
clause from the 31 st of March, 2007. As a result of that, it is possible that there is 
some diversion of industries from one State to another, but that is a direct 
consequence of the area-based exemptions provided by the previous 
Government. 
As far as what we have done is concerned, we have moved to a system of 
levying excise duty on the MRP (the maximum retail price). Now, this is a well-
accepted method. It is a non-discriminatory method and it leaves a little discretion 
on the officers so that it is transparent, neat and easily enforceable. 
Sir, we do not think that moving to a levy of excise duty on the MRP-based 
method will result in rise in prices. In fact, if you look at the wholesale price index for 
the group, drugs and medicines, on the 1st of January, 2005, the index was 
272.7, and after the change was made on the 8th of January, 2005, the figure 
which I have for 26th February, 2005, is only 272.5. In fact, there is no rise in the 
wholesale price index for the commodity 
2 

 
[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
group, drugs and medicines. In fact, a number of items have been moved 
to MRP, and wherever MRP is required to be displayed by one or other 
law, I think, the non-discriminatory and transparent method of levying excise 
duty is based on MRP with a suitable abatement. There was a 
representation that the abatement level of 35 per cent is inadequate. We 
had determined 35 per cent as the abatement level after taking into account 
the recommendations of the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers, of the 
NPPA. After considering the recommendations, although 35 per cent 
abatement was an appropriate abatement figure, in order to help the small 
scale sector, we have increased the abatement level to 40 per cent. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA Sir, I would like to bring to the 
notice of the hon. Minister a report which appeared in The Financial 
Express on March 16 and another report which appeared in The Economic 
Times of yesterday which said that the small manufacturers were opposed 
to it, especially, in Delhi. There is also another news item which appeared 
at the time of the Budget and the heading says, "Post Budget Pill — drug 
may become costlier by 2-6 per cent". I understand what the Minister has 
said about transparency. But instead of changing the excise duty from 
there to the maximum retail price, why don't the Government find a way of 
controlling the drug prices? You know the drug prices have increased in 
reality. I am talking about the retail prices. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the drug price control is a matter governed 
by the Drug Prices Control Order and that Order is administered by the 
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. So, on drug price control, the question 
must be put to my colleague. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: Sir, we put the question to the 
Government and it is the Government 's total, combined responsibility. 
Unfortunately, neither the Health Minister nor the Minister of Chemicals 
and Fertilizers is there. My question is being addressed to the Finance 
Minister. I want your protection. (Interruptions)... 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, this  coming from a former Deputy 
Chairman is ah unusual comment. Questions are put to separate 
Ministries. Now, drug price control is a matter which is dealt with by the 
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. If the hon. Member puts the question 
to that Minister, I am sure, he will answer why and under what 
circumstances the Drug Prices Control Order is being implemented. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Sir, my question to the hon. Finance Minister 
is, whether he is aware that the small manufacturers maintain a higher MRP to 
ensure a margin to the dealers or the middlemen so that they can survive in the 
competition from big multinationals and big corporate houses. When the excise 
duty is put on the MRP—I heard the hon. Minister very carefully—there is an 
administrative advantage. But while taking the administrative advantage, the 
prices of medicines will go up. That is one. Secondly, the small manufacturers 
will be put into severe trouble, so far as marketing is concerned. I would like to 
know whether the Minister is aware of this and whether the Minister is going to 
look into the situation. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, I am aware of this argument. I am aware of the 
argument put forth by the small scale manufacturers. But let us look at the facts 
and I had some examples. Take, for example, a product called Cloner-Z 0.5. The 
MRP was Rs. 148. It remains the same. The price offered for assessment under 
excise duty is Rs. 13.91. Can it be anybody's case that the clearance value under 
section 4 of the Excise Act of the drug is Rs: 13.91 for the MRP to be fixed at Rs. 
148? Can it be anybody's case that 91 per cent represents post-manufacturing 
costs? I can give you any number of examples. The assessable value is being 
kept at a very low value and as a result of which there is hardly any excise revenue. 
Therefore, whenever there is an MRP,  we take into account all post-
manufacturing costs, including retailers' margin and wholesalers' margin, and 
arrive at the abatement. We have not done this in an arbitrary fashion. We have 
asked the NPPAto do a study. The study has been done. The study reports 
that 35 per cent abatement will take care of the post-manufacturing costs. But 
when representations came, in order to be a little more generous to them, to 
give a little more allowance to them, we have increased the abatement from 35 
per cent to 40 per cent. I can give you examples of any number of drugs. Take, 
for example, a drug called Bikenrik Pharma. Now, the MRP is Rs. 210. The 
assessable value has been given as Rs. 24. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: You say the generic names so that I can 
understand what the target is. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: I don't hav e it. I have the name of the 
manufacturer. I have the name of the drug. The point I am making is that there is 
an MRP at which the consumer price is fixed. There is a value 
4 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
which they offer for excise purposes. Now, they must bear some relation. Now, we 
think that 60 per cent of MRP is a proper assessable value. If you offer only 10 per 
cent of MRP as an assessable value, how does the Excise Department 
accept that? Can 90 per cent ever be the post-manufacturing cost? Therefore, 
we have done this study. We have consulted the Ministry of Chemicals and 
Fertilisers, which is the Administrative Ministry. We have asked for a study to be 
done by the NPPA. I have got the figures of the price builp-up on many, many 
products. And, we think that 40 per cent is a generous abatement from 
MRP.

*283. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI 
RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are contemplating introduction of an internal 
audit system for all tiers of Panchayati Raj System; 
(b) the steps being taken by Govern ment to provide institutional 
framework to this system at the State and Union level; 
10 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) what will be the implications of this new institutional framework vis-
a-vis the CAG who has been auditing 30,000 crores that are flowing into 
Panchayati Raj Institutions; and 
(d) whether the proposal is part of the recommendations made at the 
Conference of the Panchayati Raj Ministers? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANISHANK ARAIYAR); 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Panchayati Raj is a State subject. The Ministry of Panchayati 
Raj is responsible for advocacy and monitoring of the implementation of 
the Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 to ensure that the State 
Panchayati Raj Acts adhere to the provisions of the Act and to endeavour 
to secure implementation in letter and spirit. As per Article 243J of the 
Constitutution "The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions 
with respect to the maintenance of accounts by the Panchayats and the 
auditing of such accounts". Therefore, it is for State Governments to identify 
the agency to get the budget/funds of Panchayats audited. The Guidelines 
issued by the Ministry of Finance for the utilization of local bodies grants 
recommended by the Eleventh Finance Commission (2000-01 to 2004-05) 
provide that the C&AG shall be res ponsible for exercising control and 
supervision over the proper maintenance of accounts and their audit for all 
the three tiers/levels of PRIs and ULBs. State Governments should send a 
request under section 20(1) of the CAG(DPC) Act, for this purpose. As per 
the Guidelines, the format for the preparation of budgets and for keeping 
accounts for local bodies shall be as prescribed by the C&AG. this subject 
has been discussed further in the sixth Round Table of Ministers in charge 
of Panchayati Raj at Guwahati On 27-28 November 2004. A copy of the 
conclusions reached during the si xth Round Table are enclosed as 
Statement-I (See below). 
In para (iv) of the conclusions of the sixth Round Table, under the heading 
audit, it has been recommended that there is need to establish an internal 
audit system at every tier of the Panchayati Raj System and to regard 
C&AG audit (or audit by bodies certified or technically guided by C&AG) 
as complementary external audit.

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
Since local bodies are now institutions of local self-government in terms of Article 
243G of the Constitution, it is necessary to upgrade the work of the Director of 
Local Fund Audit (DLFA) and other similar bodies to the level required by 
Constitutional imperatives and, to this end, for the DLFA and other similar bodies 
to work in concert with the Comptroller & Auditor General (C&AG) of India. In 
the seven Round Tables, about 150 recommendations have been made to 
strengthen Panchayats as true institutions of self government. These have been 
adopted by consensus by the Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj in the 
States at the last Round Table held at Jaipur. The Ministry has now initiated a 
process of meeting and visits to review progress in implementing these 
recommendations. These steps will continue through 2005-06 and 
subsequent year with sectoral conferences and visits to each State.

Statement-I 
Sixth Round Table of Ministers in-charge of Panchayati Raj-
Gwahati, 27-28 November2004 
Ministers in-charge of Panchayati Raj, and their representatives, bearing in mind 
the spirit of cooperative federalism which must inform the effective implementation 
of Panchayati Raj as set out in Part IX of the Constitution of India and related 
provisions, agreed to recommend to their respective governments, for joint 
acceptance by the Centre and the States, the following points of action: 
Elections 
(i) The Indian voter is one and indivisible. The principle of parity between 
parliamentary and assembly elections, on the one hand 'and 
panchayat elections, on the other, must therefore be maintained, 
especially as it is noticed that  people's participation in panchayat 
elections is substantial and generally equal to or higher than in 
parliamentary/assembly elections. Thus, for example, even in States with 
difficult geographical terrain, 88% of the electorate has participated 
in panchayat elections in Himachal Pradesh and 83.5% has participated 
in Sikkim. 
(ii) While all matters relating to panchayat elections have been vested by the 
Constitution in State legislature/governments, there is need 
12 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to work towards commonality, if not uniformity, in election procedures and 
provisions. To this end, it would desirable to vest all responsibilities for the 
election process in State Election Commissions rather than splitting 
these up, including: 
(a) preparation of electoral rolls; 
(b) delimitation of constituencies;  
(c) reservations and rotations; 
(d) qualifications of candidates;  
(e) conduct of elections; and 
(f) functioning as the first stage of adjudication in election disputes. 
(iii) The Union Government might consider the preparation of a model code 
relating to the supervision, direction and conduct of elections to the 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) 
(rv) With a view to evolving a common electoral roll for all levels of 
elections, consultations between the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) 
and the State Election Commissioners(SECs) might be encouraged 
with a view to resolving pratical problems that might arise in the 
preparation, maintenance and updating of such electoral rolls for electionsto 
be held at different times for differ ent levels of Governments. The 
panchayat and nagarpalika wards should be regarded as the building 
blocks for electoral rolls for all levels of election. 
(v) Consideration may be given to incorporating in the laws pertaining to PR 
elections the same provisions of disclosure as apply to Parliament and State 
Assembly Elections. 
(vi) The Election Commission of India (ECl) might be approached for 
establishing a forum for institutional interaction between SECs and ECl on 
issues such as directives being issued by the State Election Commission; 
the use of radio broadcasting for disseminating election-related information; 
anomalies arising out of migration; linking delimitation with census 
operation; uniformity in service condition of SECs; and proposals like sealing 
the electronic chip in the Electronic Voting Machine (EVM), and not the 
machine itself, for evidentiary 
13 

 
RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
purposes, thus leaving the machine free for use in Panchayat 
elections. 
(vii) States may consider according the same salary and emoluments to 
State Election Commissioners as High Court Judges are entitled to. 
(viii) It is recommended that the Delimitation Commission be regularly in 
contaot with the SEC's, who are members of the Commission, to 
sort out practical difficulties arising out of delimitation process. 
(ix) To facilitate the use of Elec tronic Voting Machines (EVMs) in 
Panchayat elections, the Union Government in consultation with 
Election Commission of India and the SECs, might consider issues 
relating to the funding of the purchase of EVMs for the use of State 
Election Commissions. 
(x) Elections to District Planning Committees provided for in Article 
243ZD of the Constitution might also be brought within the purview of 
State Election Commissions to ensure full conformity with 
Constitutional provisions, which has not always been the case. 
Audit 
(i) Since local bodies are now institutions of local self-government, it is 
necessary to upgrade the work of the Director of Local. Fund Audit 
(DLFA) and other similar bodies to the level required by Constitutional 
imperatives and, to this end, for DLFA and other similar bodies to 
work in concert with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India 
(C&AG). 
(ii) In recognition of PRIs being inst itutions of local self-government, 
PRIs themselves should be associated with the preparation of 
standards and norms and the emphasis should be on fund 
management and fund tracking, rather than simply on fundflow, to 
ensure greater accountability. 
(iii) In order to ensure that such audit contributes effectively to capping, 
reducing and eventually eliminat ing the scope for corruption in 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRI s), it is necessary that audit & 
accounting standards appropriate to the work of the Panchayats be 
established and observed. These standards should be elementary, 
14 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
simple and easily comprehensible to the elected representatives, 
and should focus on: 
- when transactions should be looked into; 
- what should be monitored; 
- how the transactions should be documented; and 
- how they should be disclosed. 
(iv) There is need to establish an internal audit system at every tier of 
the Panchayati Raj system and to regard C&AG audit (or audit by 
bodies certified or technically guided by C&AG) as complementary 
external audit. 
(v) Audit, to be effective, might include the establishment of a National 
Accounting Standards Board (NASB) for local government accounts 
and be complemented by the establishment of audit commissions 
or similar such regulatory bodies at the State level. 
(vi) Besides, arrangements may be made in State Legislatures for the 
establishment of Public Accounts Committees (PACs) specifically 
for PRIs or for the accounts of PRIs to be submitted to PR Committees 
of the State Legislatures. State level committees, as in Andhra 
Pradesh; for the settlement of audit paras may also be considered. 
(vii) It may be useful to complement such institutional arrangements by 
legislating an appropriate Fiscal Responsibility Act for elected local 
authorities. 
(viii) Outsourcing of accounting by such measures as village panchayats 
being authorized to employ certified Chartered Accountants against 
standard contracts might be considered. 
(ix) The training of both officials and elected representatives in sound 
accounting and audit practices is a high priority. To this end, State 
Governments are invited to make full use of the Regional Training 
Institutes(RTIs) functioning under the aegis of the C &AG in particular 
the RTI at Kolkata which has been declared a centre of excellence; 
as also of the Institute of Public Auditors of India (IPAI). Substantial 
additional funding from the Union Government to facilitate training is 
a high priority. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
(x) Those State Governments which have not as yet availed of the 
arrangements for bringing the C&AG into the exercise of accounting and 
audit, including the C&AG's Technical Guidance and Supervision (TGS) 
Scheme for the PRIs, are invited to do so and the attention of all concerned 
is drawn to the publications of  the Indian and Audit Accounts 
Department, in particular: 
(a) Auditing Standards for PRIs and Urban Local Bodies 
(b) Guidelines for Certification of Audit of Accounts of PRIs 
(c) Training module of Audit of Gram Panchayats 
(xi) Given the shortage of staff for undertaking formal accounts and audit work in 
the lakhs of Village Panchayats, thousands of Intermediate Panchayats 
and hundreds of Zilla Parishads around the country, it is essential that 
automation and computerization of accounts be undertaken with all 
deliberate speed and to this end software like the one being prepared by 
the Xavier Institute of Management, Bhubaneshwar for the Orissa State 
Government, for maintaining day-to-day accounts, which is expected to be 
ready by early 2004, be deployed as widely as possible 
everywhere. 
(xii) Social audit is an important complement to formal audit and for the sound 
and healthy development of Panchayati Raj, it is essential to establish a 
symbiotic relationship between social and formal audit. 
(xiii) Social audit must necessarily be undertaken at the level of the Gram 
Sabha but might also be undertaken at higher levels of the Panchayat 
Raj system, as in West Bengal. 
(xiv) For social audit to be effective and based on the best practices 
available in different States, c onsideration might be given to the 
preparation of Social Audit Policies for adoption by State Legislatures/ 
Governments so as to provide a framework within which social audit is 
undertaken. Such Social Audit Policies may be targeted at facilitating 
popular participation in fighting corruption in Panchayats, as also 
complementing formal audit processes by quality assessment, 
ascertainment of preferences and the provision of choices. At the same 
time, Social Audit Policies may provide for institutional measures to 
prevent needless harassment 
(xv) To ensure appropriate follow-up to issues raised through social audit, 
legislative bodies and regulatory authorities might treat social audit 
16 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
resolutions on par with formal audit paras to ensure consideration 
and disposal within a time-bound framework. 
(xvi) Given the critical importance of  total disclosure of information for 
effective social audit, States might consider passing Right to 
Information legislation, taking into account the legislation already on 
the books in such States as Rajasthan.

Statement 
(a) Article 243 G of the Constitution deals with the powers, authority 
and responsiblities of Panchayats. It provides that subject to the provisions

The Pradhans and other authorities under the three tier of system of

implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development in association with the 
Panchayati Raj Institutions at the levels of district, block and village. This 
scheme aims at the generation of additional wage employment and thus 
providing social and economic assets and rural infrastructure development. 
Funds and foodgrains allocated to a district are distributed amongst District 
Panchayat, Intermediate Panchayats and Village Panchayats in the ratio 
of 20:30:50. During the current year, an amount of Rs. 4,500 crores and 50 
lakh tonnes foodgrains have been allocated under this programme. In 
addition to this, a new programme called the National Food for Work 
Programme has been launched in November, 2004 in the 150 most 
backward districts with an allocation of Rs. 2020 crores and 20 lakh tonnes 
foodgrains with a view to ensuring a larger number of days of employment 
opportunity to the rural poor in these selected districts.

(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard; 
(c) whether Government consider the demand for price hike made by 
the oil companies justified; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) the action Government propose to take in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (e) A Statem ent is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir.  
(b) to (e) The year 2004-05 witnessed the highest rise in oil prices 
international markets in recent times. As compared to the average Indian 
basket crude price of US$ 27.98/barrel during 2003-04, the average price 
during 2004-05 (April 2004-January 2005) has been US$37.87/barrel. During 
February and first fort night of March it has been as high as US$42.67/ 
barrel and US$48.98/barrel respectively. With a view to containng the burden 
of the increase in international prices on consumers of PDS kerosene, 
domestic LPG, diesel and petrol, it was decided that the burden should be 
equitably shared also by the Government and Oil Companies. Thus, 
Government reduced the excise duty on petrol, diesel and domestic LPG 
by 4%, 3% and 8%, resepectively effe ctive 16.6.04. Further, effective 
19.8.04, the excise duty on petrol, diesel and PDS Kerosene was reduced 
by 3%, 3% and 4% resepctively. The Government also reduced customes 
duty by 5% each on petrol, diesel, PDS Kerosene and Domestic LPG 
with effect from 19/8/04. In the Budget 2005-06, the following changes 
have, inter alia, been announced effective 1.3.2005: 
Customs Duties 
- Reduction in customs duty on crude from 10% to 5% 
- Reduction in Customts duty on domestic LPG and PDS Kerosene 
from 5% to nil. 
- Reduction in customs duty on other petroleum products were from 
15%-20% to 10%. 
30 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Excise Duties 
- Reduction in excise duty on Domestic LPG from 8% to nil and on 
PDS Kerosene from 12% to nil. 
In addition to these fiscal measures, the following administrative 
measures have been taken: 
(i) PDS kerosene and domestic LPG are subsidized products. In addition 
to Government subsidy, public sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) have been sharing the burden by not passing the full increase 
in the international prices in the domestic consumer prices of these 
products. Under-recoveries on this account are estimated around 
Rs. 18,000 crore in the current fiscal year, 2004-05. 
(ii) There has been no increase in the price of PDS kerosene since 
April, 2002; Diesel and LPG prices have been frozen since midnight 
of 4/5 November 2004, and petrol since midnight of 14/15 November, 
2004. 
As regards burden sharing by Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) they 
have not passed on the full increase in the international prices in the 
domestic consumer prices of these products. The prices of petrol and 
diesel in the country are fixed on the principle of import parity. The total 
under-recoveries to OMCs due to non-revision of prices of petrol and 
diesel for the period 1st April, 2004 to 15th March, 2005 are estimated at 
Rs. 1526 crore. 
The pricing mechanism for petrol, diesel, PDS Kerosene and Domestic 
LPG during 2004-05 has attempted to balance the interests of various 
stakeholders, viz., Consumers, Government and oil companies. The burden 
borne by oil companies will, of course, go up to the extent that domestic 
prices are not revised upwards when international prices shoot up, but it 
is hoped that when international prices stabilise the price band mechanism 
might be restored, thus moderating the burden of under-recoveries on oil 
companies.

(a) and (b) No, Sir. The Tsunami disaster has not significantly affected 
the tourism industry in South India and tourist arrivals to the country have 
not been adversely affected due to t he Tsunami. None of the affected 
State Governments / Union territories has reported loss of life of tourists 
due to the Tsunami Some damage to tourism properties has been reported 
by them, as per details given below: 
(i) Andaman & Nicobar Islands: Most of the damage has occurred in

Tsunami.

Kochi, Muzhippilangad and the Ashtamudi Backwater Front have 
been affected. 
(iv) Pondicherry: Some damage reported to the St. James Court Beach 
Resort, Chunnambar resort, Hotel Pondicherry Ashok and Dolphin 
Beach, Seagulls Restaurant and Water Sports Complex in Karaikal 
Region and Boat Club and Seagulls Restaurant in Yanam Region. 
(v) Tamil Nadu : Tourist cottages / beach resorts, hotels, boat jetty, 
launches, tourist amenities, view to wer, beach facilities, etc. at 
Mamallapuram, Muttukadu, Kanyakumari, Mudaliyarkuppam, 
Nagapattinam, Velankanni and Poompuhar have been damaged. 
(c) The affected States / Union Territories are undertaking work of re-
building of the damages tourist properties. The Ministry of Tourism assists 
State Governments / Union Territories by providing Central Financial 
Assistance for tourism projects and infrastructure, based on specific 
proposals submitted by the State Governments / Union Territories. The 
Ministry of tourism has taken initiatives / promotional measures to keep 
the trade, consumer and media overseas briefed in order to reinforce the 
image of India as a safe destination for travel.

Statement 
(a) and (b) The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) 
Act, 2003 mandates the Central Government to eliminate revenue deficit 
by end-March, 2009 and reduce fiscal deficit to not more than 3 per cent of 
gross domestic product (GDP) at curr ent market prices. Elimination of 
fiscal deficit is not an objective under the Act. The Fiscal Responsibility 
and Budget Management Rules, 2004 specify the minimum annual fiscal 
corrections that need to be achieved in pursuance of the above targets. 
The Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement (MTFPS) and Fiscal Policy 
Strategy Statement, which were presented to Parliament along with the 
Annual Financial Statement and Demand for Grants, respectively specify 
the fiscal correction path in the medium term and the strategy to be adopted 
in achieving the fiscal correction budgeted for 2005-06. 
(c) and (d) Government proposes to  achieve the fiscal correction 
mandated under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 
2003, primarily through improvement in the tax-GDP ratio. Containing 
unproductive expenditure is also anothe r important element in fiscal 
consolidation. Government propose to contain the rapid growth in committed 
revenue expenditure like interest payments, pensions, and untargeted 
subsidies through appropriate policies and annual priorities to this effect.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) The Reserve Bank of India 
(RBI) in its Report on Currency and Finance, 2003-04, points out that 
opening up of the services to international trade and remittances flows 
have accelerated global intergration. This has implications for the conduct

report also observes that a more serious challenge to the conduct of 
monetary policy emerges from the capital account. The report mentions

surpluses in the current account. Indi cating that these external sector 
developments have influenced conduct of monetary policy, the report points 
out that a multi-pronged approach has been followed in India for managing 
capital flows to ensure domestic ec onomic and financial  stability. The 
main features of this approach include; liberlization of policies relating to 
capital account outflows, encouraging pre-payment of external borrowings; 
alignment of interest rates on non-resident deposits; and greater exchange 
rate flexibility. The report further states that these measures have been 
supplemented with sterilization operations to minimize inflationary impact 
of capital flows and ensure financial stability.

White Paper on disinvestment 
2221. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to prepare and issue a 
comprehensive white paper on disinvestment; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) by when the white paper is likely to be issued; 
(d) the basic differences between the disinvestment policy of the present 
Government and the one pursued by the previous Government; and 
(e) whether steps are being taken in this context to ensure that the profit 
making public sector undertakings are left out of the disinvestment plan and are 
given full managerial and commercial autonomy for effective functioning? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The White Paper is under preparation and will be tabled in 
Parliament during the forthcoming Monsoon Session. 
(d) The focus of the disinvestment policy has changed from the earlier one, 
emphasizing Strategic Sale, to a broad based strategy encompassing the 
disinvestment of minority shareholding in profitable PSEs, while retaining at least 
51% shareholding and full management control with the Government, 
restructuring and modernisation of loss making but revivable Public Sector 
Undertakings, including through the induction of a Private Investor and closure 
or sale of chronically sick PSEs, after ensuring that the dues of the employees 
alongwith compensation are paid. The Disinvestment Commission has been 
wound up in October, 2004. The Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector 
Enterprises has been constituted by the Government, which is located in the 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), to take up the cases of strengthening, 
modernizing, reviving and restructuring of Public Sector Enterprises. Greater 
transparency will be ensured in the utilisation of the proceeds from disinvestment,

permanent corpus while the income from the fund will be used for investment in

companies will be retained in the Public Sector. Government is committed 
to devolve full managerial and commercial autonomy to successful, profit 
making PSEs, operating in a competitive environment, which will generally 
not be privatised, though these PSEs may approach the capital markets 
for raising resources and Government may sell minority shareholding in 
these companies, retaining at least 51% shareholding, so as not to alter 
their public sector character.

(c) The reasons for slow progress under the PMRY scheme are attributed 
to lack of viable and income generating activities and also reaching the 
saturation level of popular activities, non-soonsor of quality loan applications 
by Task Force Committee, delay in obtaining necessary clearance for 
undertaking the activity from different Government agencies, lack of proper 
coordination and cooperation from Government Department and poor 
recovery position. 
(d) RBI and Government of India have initiated the following steps for 
improvement of performance under PMRY and other allied schemes. 
(i) Banks have been advised to carry out scrutiny of rejected 
applications by a higher authority from their controlling/Head Office. 
(ii) Banks have been instructed to dispose of applications for loans 
upto Rs. 25,000 within 2 weeks and upto Rs. 2 lakh within 4 
weeks, provided the loan applications are complete in all respects. 
(iii) Time frames have been laid down for receipt of applications from 
the DICs to banks and thereafter sanction and disbursements of 
loans by banks. 
(iv) Banks have been instructed to se t-up training institutes jointly 
with the State Governments by utilizing the existing infrastructure

PAN Mandatory for purchasing Credit cards 
2235 SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that his Ministry has issued a notification making PAN 
mandatory for buying a credit card, making investments in mutual funds, 
shares, bonds, debentures, etc; 
(b) if so, the reasons behind this move; and 
(c) what would be the position of minors who are not Income Tax-payers and are 
not having PAN and wish to buy credit card, etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. Vide Notification dated 1st December, 
2004, quoting of PAN has been made mandatory in respect of the following 
transactions:— 
131 

 
RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
(i) buying a credit card; 
(ii) making payment of Rs. 50,000/- or more to a Mutual Fund for purchase 
of its units; 
(iii) making payment of Rs. 50,000/- or more to a company for acquiring 
shares issued by it; 
(iv) making payment of Rs. 50,000/- or more to a company or an institution 
for acquiring debentures or bonds issued by it; 
(v) making payment of Rs. 50,000/- or more to the Reserve Bank of 
India for acquiring bonds issued by it. 
(b) PAN is a unique identification number provided to an assessee. 
Therefore, compulsory quoting of PAN in the above transactions will facilitate 
collation and verification of information received through Annual information 
Return. This will enable the Income-tax department to reduce interface 
with public for collection of information. This measure will also widen the 
tax base. 
(c) a minor is not required to have a PAN if he does not have any 
income other than income includible in the income of his parents. In the 
case of a credit card issued in the name of a minor, as "add-on" to the 
guardian, the PAN of the guardian is required to be quoted. 
Installation of ATMs by Banks 
2236. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Automatic Teller Machines (ATMs) have 
proved useful and economical to Banks; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for not installing ATMs by Nationalised 
Banks in every city specially NCT of Delhi; and 
(c) what are the numbers of ATMs, being installed during the next one 
year by various Banks in NCT of Delhi, area-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S>S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. ATMs are useful to the 
customers/public, as they provide round the clock access to the customers 
132 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
for limited banking facilities. Further, working of ATMs does not require 
deployment of any manpower and has a lower infrastructural cost in 
comparison to a full-fledged branch. 
(b) and (c) At present, more than six hundred ATMs of all public sector 
banks are functioning in NCT of Delhi. As per the extant policy, banks are 
free to install ATMs at places of their choice. The banks are not required to 
obtain prior permission of the Reserve Bank of India for installation of on 
site/off site ATMs. As installation of ATMs is a purely business decision of 
the managements of the Banks, it is not possible to say how many ATMs 
will be installed during the next one year.

Wanchoo Committee Report on Black Money 
2241. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per report of Wanchoo Committee, the 
generation of black money in India works out 55 per cent of Gross Domestic 
Product; 
(b) if so, what is Government's proposal to deal with this problem; and 
(c) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) The Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
(Wanchoo Committee) in its Final Report of December, 1971 estimated black 
income at Rs. 1800 crore for the year 1968-69 which works out to 16.3% of 
the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). 
(b) and (c) The Government takes several deterrant and punitive 
measures to prevent the generation and flow of black money. These include 
undertaking search and seizure and surveys, scrutiny of returns, imposition of 
penalty and launching of prosecution in appropriate cases. In order to unearth 
balck money in the ecomony, the Government has in the past introduced 
various voluntary disclousre schemes. 
Further in order to deal with the problem of black money, Finance Bill, 
2005 has proposed the following measures:— 
(i) Levy of tax @ 0.1% on withdrawal of cash on a single day of over Rs. 
10,000 or more from banks; 
(ii) Banks would be required to report to the Government all deposits which 
are exempt from Tax Deduction at Source on interest.

have proliferated to Rs. 1,15,000 crores a year which roughly comes to

percolate to the poorest sections of the population, or the beneficiaries

Performance of Kisan Credit Card scheme 
2245. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what has been the performance so far of the Kisan Credit Card 
schemes and the extent of its acceptance by farmers; 
(b) what is the credit limit and the rate of interest under the scheme; 
(c) whether the scheme is available throughout the country and if not, the 
reasons therefor; and

of the country and if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme has emerged 
as a widely accepted mechanism for delivery of hassle-free crop loan to farmers. 
The scheme introduced in August, 1998 as an innovative credit delivery 
mechanism, has been progressing satisfactorily. About 4.80 crore KCCs have 
been issued till 31st January, 2005. The scope of the scheme has been 
recently enlarged to cover the term loans for agriculture and allied activities 
including a reasonable component to meet consumption needs besides the 
existing facility of providing crop loan limit. 
140 

[22 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) No ceiling has been envisaged for sanction of credit limit under the 
scheme. However, the banks may fix t he credit limit to farmers on the 
basis of their land holding, cropping pattern and scale of finance 
recommended by the District Level Technical Committee. The Co-operative 
Banks also take into account the individual maximum borrowing power 
fixed by the Registrar of the Co-operative Societies while fixing the credit 
limit under the scheme which may vary from State to State. As the interest 
rate regime has been deregulated by the Reserve Bank of India, banks

Exemption of citizens of Sikkim from income tax 
†2251. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that at the time of merger of Sikkim with Indian in 
1975 it was committed that citizens of Sikkim would be exempted from 
income tax and direct taxes; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to impose income tax 
and other taxes on the citizens of Sikkim against the said commitment; 
(c) whether Government have received any memorandum from the State 
Government of Sikkim; 
(d) if so, whether Government are considering the same; and 
(e) the details of the memorandum received from Sikkim? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) Article 371F was inserted in the 
Constitution of India by the Constitution (36th Amendment) Act, 1975, with 
effect from 26.04.1975, introducing special provisions with regard to the 
State of Sikkim. The Article, inter alia, provides that notwithstanding 
anything in the Constitution of India, all laws in force immediately before 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2005] 
the appointed day in the territories comprised in the State of Sikkim shall 
continue to be in force therein until amended or repealed. However, Clause 
(n) of the said Article provides that the President may, by public notification, 
extend with such restrictions or modifications as he thinks fit to the State 
of Sikkim any enactment which is in force in a State of India at the date of 
the notification. 
Pursuant to the above Constitutional amendment, the Ministry of Home 
Affairs issued a notification number S.O.1028(E) dated 7th November, 
1988, whereby direct tax laws of India including the Income-tax Act, 1961, 
the Gift Tax Act, 1958 and the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 were extended to the 
State of Sikkim with effect from assessment year 1989-90. Further, through 
the Finance Act, 1989, the effective date of implementation of the direct 
tax laws to Sikkim was extended to assessment year 1990-91.

on 17.06.2004 requesting, inter alia, expeditious resolution of the impasse

well as the Government of India. The recommendations of the Committee
