Meeting of inter-State Co-ordination Committee 
†2375. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a meeting of the inter-State Co-ordination 
Committee was held recently; 
(b) if so, the suggestions received to ch eck crimes in the National Capital 
Territory; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to implement these suggestions and by 
when these suggestions are likely to be implemented? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI S. 
REGUPATHY): (a) to (c) The last meeting of the inter-State Co-ordination 
Committee was held on 6th January, 2005 'under the chairmanship of the Lt. Governor 
of Delhi. The main suggestions given in the meeting to check crimes in the National 
Capital Territory of Delhi and the action taken thereon are indicated below: 
Suggestion—Zonal Integrated Police Net (ZIPNET) can work as a hub for sharing 
information, data, photographs etc. This concept of exchange of information can, in the 
coming year, be further extended to videoconferencing. 
Action Taken—Delhi Police has already started feeding the information relating to the 
following subjects: 
(i) Descriptibn of un-identified dead bodies to match with missing persons; 
(ii) Sharing of information regarding day-to-day crimes reported; 
(iii) Accessibility to Crime and Criminal Databases of each other; 
(iv) Press releases relating to crime having inter-State ramifications; 
(v) Information about prevailing crime trend among cities/States; 
(vi) Exchange of dossiers of criminals electronically without losing time and 
sharing of daily crime bulletin; 
(vii) Flashing of information and description of suspect; 
(viii) Flashing of portraits of suspects; and 
(ix) Flashing of information about unclaimed and stolen vehicles. 
Extension of videoconferencing in the coming years depends on examination of 
its technical and economical feasibility. 
Suggestion—Development of technology and communication systems should be 
improved, as the criminals are not restricted to geographical boundaries. 
Action Taken—A number of steps have been taken to strengthened the communication 
network within the National Capital Region including a direct wireless link provided to all the 
District Control Rooms of neighbouring States where any information of significance is 
transmitted immediately. 
108 

[23 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Suggestion— The meeting of Inter-St ate Co-ordination Committee should 
be followed up by meetings between officers of Delhi and the neighbouring 
States at more functional level. 
Action Taken— Meetings with neighbouring States are being organized 
regularly. Delhi Police is working as a Secretariat to organize such meetings. Besides 
meetings held under the chairmanship of Lt. Governor of Delhi, meetings are 
also held at the level of (i) Commissioner of Police where Inspector Generals of 
Police and other senior officers of the neighbouring States participate, and (ii) at 
the level of District Deputy Commissioners of Police with their counterparts in 
the neighbouring States. 
Suggestion— There is a need to set up an effective exchange system with the 
use of advance technology. 
Action Taken— Delhi Police is already cooperating with neighbouring States 
and providing all significant intelligence inputs to them Compact Discs (CDs) 
containing information relating to crimes and criminals are regularly sent to 
the neighbouring States. 
Suggestion—As the criminals were getting better organized, it had become 
imperative to combine resources and to  carry out joint operations to make 
policing more effective. 
Action Taken— Delhi Police is already organizing joint operations with the 
police force of neighbouring States. A number of such operations have been 
carried out in the past. 
Suggestion— Officers of Intelligence"Bureau and Narcotics Control Bureau 
may be associated in the meetings of the inter-State Co-ordination Committee. 
Action Taken— Officers of Intelligen ce Bureau and Narcotics Control 
Bureau are consulted as and when necessary. 
Suggestion— There was an increase in motor vehicle thefts, highway 
robberies, snatchings etc. in which organized gangs were involved. Therefore, 
there was a need for sharing information and conducting joint operations to 
identify these gangs. Co-ordination meetings may be organized at the district 
level also. 
Action Taken— Delhi Police is sharing information about crime and 
criminals, organizing joint operations and holding co-ordination meetings at 
district level. 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
Suggestion—There was a need of computerization of Transport 
Department records, in view of the increase of motor vehicle thefts. 
Action Taken—Records of Transport Department have already been 
computerized. Delhi Police is having its own database containing information 
regarding ownership and other details which are provided to all police forces as and 
when required. 
Suggestion—The ZIPNET has vast potential and it can also be used for 
chatting, exchange of photographs etc. and senior police officers are required to 
take personal interest in its optimum utilization. 
Action Taken—The senior officers of  Delhi Police have evinced keen 
interest in optimum utilization of the ZIPNET.

Unsafe structures in Delhi 
2391. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any survey has been conducted to find out the unsafe 
structures facing fire hazards in Delhi; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of preventive steps being taken to keep check on 
construction materials and structural safety? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a.) to (c) Yes, Sir. A survey was conducted at the 
time of enactment of the Delhi Fire Prevention and Fire Safety Act, 1986 
wherein 220 buildings were identified which lacked the requisite fire 
protection measures. Subsequently, fire safety equipments were installed in 
217 of these buildings. Of the remaining three, one was sealed and electricity 
and water supply of the remaining two were disconnected. 
Another survey was conducted by the Chief Fire Officer in pursuance of 
order passed by the High Court of Delhi on 23rd August, 2004 in CM No. 
6904/2004 in CWP No. 2710 of 1998 titled Dr. B.L. Wadhera Vs. 
Government of NCT of Delhi and others, wherein 2506 buildings constructed 
after 1983 in Lal Dora, Extended Lal Dora and Non-LSI Dora areas were 
identified lacking the necessary fire protection arrangements. The owners of these 
buildings were advised through notices published in newspapers on 17th/18th 
September, 2004 to install fire safety measures in these buildings within 90 
days. 
(d) As per the provisions of the Delhi Building Bye-Laws, 1983, it is 
mandatory to obtain 'clearance' from the Delhi Fire Service for construction and No 
Objection Certificate (NOC) for occupancy in respect of the following types 
of buildings: 
(i) All buildings having height of 15 metres and more; and 
(ii) Buildings of less than 15 metres housing assembly, institutions, 
industries, storage and hospitals. 
At the time of sanction of building plans, a structural safety certificate from 
the Structural Engineer is obtained as per the amendment made in Building 
Bye-Laws vide Notification dated 21st March, 2001. This includes construction 
materials. At the time of grant of occu pancy certificate, a certificate is also 
obtained from the owner, duly signed by Architect and Structural Engineer, 
certifying that construction is as per relevant Indian Standard code.

Increasing the per capita availability of power  
2420. DR. VIJAY MALLYA: 
SHRI LALIT SURI:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a decision has been taken by Government to increase per capita availability 
of power over 1000 Units as against present availability -of 500 units; 
(b) what is the requirement of funds to achieve this target; 
(c) how the funds for the purpose are proposed to be raised; and 
(d) what are the other salient features of the policy and the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) Yes Sir. The National 
Electricity Policy notified on 12th February, 2005 under the provisions of Section 3 of 
the Electricity Act, 2003, envisages increase of per capita availability of power to over 1000 
units by 2012. 
(b) To meet the objective of rapid economic growth and "power for all" 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
including completion of household electrification, the need for investment of about Rs. 
9,00,000 crores in generation, transmission, sub-transmission, distribution and rural 
electrification had been estimated in the 10th and 11th Plan periods. 
(c) Public sector investments, both at the Central Government and State Governments, has 
been envisaged and the need for attracting substantial private investment has been 
highlighted. 
(d) Salient features of the policy are given in the enclosed Statement. 
Statement 
Salient features of the National Electricity Policy 
1. Aims at accelerated development of power sector, providing supply of electricity to 
all areas and protecting interests of consumers and other stakeholders. 
2. Objectives: 
* Access to Electricity—Available for all households in next five 
years. 
* I Availability of Power—Demand to be fully met by 2012. Energy 
and peaking shortages to be overcome and spinning reserve to be available. 
* Supply of Reliable and Quality Power of specified standards in an efficient 
manner and at reasonable rates. 
* Per capita availability of electricity to be increased to over 1000 units by 
2012. 
* Minimum lifeline consumption of 1 unit/household/day as a merit good 
by year 2012. 
* Financial Turnaround and Commercial Viability of electricity Sector. 
* Protection of consumers' interests. 
 
3. CEA to notify first National Electricity Plan in six months with a perspective 
up 12th Plan period. The Plan prepared by CEA to be used by prospective 
generating companies, transmission utilities and transmission/distribution 
licensees as reference document. 
4. Development of Rural Electrification Distribution backbone, village electrification 
and household electrification to achieve the NCMP 
162 

[23 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
target of completing household electrification in next five years. 
Financial support in terms of capital subsidy to States for rural 
electrification. Special preference to Dalit Bastis, Tribal Areas and other 
weaker sections for rural electrification. REC to be nodal agency for 
rural electrification at Central Government level. 
5. Creation of adequate generation capacity with a spinning reserve of at least 
5% by 2012 with availability of installed capacity at 85%. 
6. Full development of hydro potential. Provision of long tenor finance for 
these projects. 
7. Choice of fuel for thermal generation to be based on economics of 
generation and supply of electricity. 
8. Development of National Grid. 
9. Cost of recovery of service from consumers at tariff reflecting efficient costs 
to ensure financial viability of the sector 
 
10. Provision of support to lifeline consumers (households below poverty line 
having consumption of 3d units per month) in terms of tariffs. 
11. Availability Based Tariff (ABT) to be extended to State level for better grid 
discipline through economic signaling. 
 
12. Special emphasis on time bound reduction of transmission and 
distribution losses.  
13. Measures to promote competition aimed at consumer benefits. 
14. Reliability and quality of power supply to be monitored by State 
Elecetricity Regulatory Commissions. 
15. Exploitation of non-conventional energy sources such as small hydro, 
solar, biomass and wind for additional power generation capacity. 
Other Features 
16. Emphasis on achieving higher efficiency levels of generating plants 
through necessary renovation and modernization. 
17. Central Government to facilitate the continued development of 
national grid. CTU and STU to undertake coordinated planning and 
development. 
18. Transmission capacity to have redundancy level and margins as per 
international standards. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
 
 per international standards. 
19. Adequate transitional financial support for reforming power utilities. 
Encouragement for private sector participation in distribution. 
20. The State Regulatory Commissions to put in place independent third party 
meter testing arrangement. 
21. Support for adoption of IT system for ensuring correct billing to consumers. 
22. Speedy implementation of stringent measures against theft of electricity. 
23. Full emphasis on augmentation of R&D base. Mission approach for identified 
priorities areas. 
24. Demand side management through energy conservation measures. Labels regarding 
energy efficiency to be displayed on appliances. Efficient agricultural pumpsets 
and efficient lighting technologies to be promoted. Appropraite tariff structure for 
managing the peak load. 
25. Special attention for developing training infrastructure in the field of regulation; 
trading and power market. 
26. For giving boost to renewable and non-conventional energy sources, a prescribed 
percentage of power, as pecified by State Regulatory Commissions, to be 
purchased from such sources of energy at the earliest 
27. Necessary regulations and appointing Ombudsman for redressal of consumers' 
grievances to be in place in six months. 
Electrification of one lakh villages and one crore households 
2421. SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the annual targets of Government's programme of 
electrification of one lakh villages and one crore households by the year 
2012 and the year-wise financial outlay for this purpose; and 
(b) the names of the agencies implementing the scheme, their obligations 
and means to achieve the target? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) Anew scheme of 
rural electricity Infrastructure and Household Electrification has 
164 

[23 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
been approved for the attainment of the National Common Minimum Programme of 
completing Rural Household Electrification in five years by replacing the earlier 40% 
Capital Subsidy Scheme. Under this scheme 90% Capital Subsidy would be 
provided for: 
(i) Creation of Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) with one 33/11 
Kv (or 66/11 kV) substation in every block appropriately linked to the State 
Transmission System. 
(ii) Creation of Village Electricity Infrastructure (VEI) for electrification of all un-
electrified villages/habitations with distribution transformer(s) in 
every village/habitation. 
(iii) Decentralized Distributed Generation (DDG) and Supply System for 
Villages/Habitations where grid supply is not cost effective and where 
Ministry of Non-Conventional energy Sources would not be providing 
electricity through their programme(s). 
(iv) Electrification of all un-elect rified Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
households in the country free of charge. 
The estimated expenditure for 1st phase of the Scheme is Rs. 5000 crore for the 
remaining period of 10th Plan. 
The scheme would be implemented through the Rural Electrification Corporation 
(REC), a Public Sector Undertaking under this Ministry. The services of Central Public 
Sector Undertakings have been offered to States who would like to use them for execution 
of projects under this scheme and the modalities have been worked out in the 
Memorandum of Understanding that REC has entered into with NTPC, POWERGRID, 
NHPC and DVC to make available CPSUs' project management expertise and 
capabilities to States wishing to use their services.

Guidelines for power purchasing policy 
2427. SHRI SUDARSHAN AKARAPU: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has formulated any guidelines with regard to power 
purchase policy entered into by State Governments with various private independent 
producers for supplying power; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (c) As per the 
provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions 
have been given the responsibility of regulating electricity purchase and procurement 
process of distribution licenses including the price at which electricity shall be procured 
from the generating companies or licensees or from other sources through agreements 
for purchase of power for distribution and supply within the State. 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 further provides that the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff has been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central 
Government. Central Government has issued the guidelines for competitive bidding for 
determination of tariff for procurement of power by distribution licensees. The 
guidelines provide both for long term procurement of electricity for a period of 7 years 
and above and also for medium term procurement for a period ranging from one to seven 
years.

Reforms for the State of Maharashtra on 2nd July, 2003, a decision was taken to prepare a

of rural habitations through a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, namely 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP).

weightage for rural population, 35% for hydrological conditions, 15% for 
NC/PC villages and 10% for quality affected villages. The State Government can

5% of ARWSP funds are ear-marked for rural water supply in DDP areas and 
Rajasthan get funds in proportion to the number of NSS habitation without safe 
sources. 
Apart from these, 5% of total ARWSP funds are released for meeting 
contingencies arising out of natural cal amities and emergent situations like 
drought etc.

proportionate annual allocation of funds to the State.

provides for the following: 
"(1) The Central Government shall, by notification, establish a fund to be 
called the National Employment Guarantee Fund for the purposes of 
this Act. 
(2) The Central Government may, after due appropriation made by 
Parliament by law in this behalf, credit by way of grants or loans such 
sums of money as the Central Government may consider necessary to 
the National Fund. 
(3) The amount standing to be credit of the National Fund shall be 
utilized in such manner and subject to such conditions and limitations as may 
be prescribed by the Central Government." 
(e) Clause 24(1) of the Bill provides that the Central Govt, may, in 
consultation with the Comptroller and Au ditor General of India, prescribed 
appropriate arrangements for audits of the accounts of the scheme at all levels. 
Employment opportunities under EGS 
†2452. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH:  Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of opportunities of employments provided through the 
Employment Guarantee Scheme; 
(b) the nature of such opportunities of employment; 
(c) whether the opportunities of employment provided under the scheme are 
permanent; and 
(d) the details of per capita/per day income generated through such 
opportunities of employment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) to (c) The National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 introduced in the Lok Sabha on 
21.12.2004 provides for atleast 100 days of guaranteed wage employment in every 
financial year to rural poor households, whose adult members volunteer to do 
unskilled manual work, in areas where the proposed legislation will be 
applicable.

(d) As the Bill has been referred to the Standing Committee on Rural 
Development and has so far not been enacted, it is not possible to estimate per 
capita/per day income generated through the opportunities of employment 
provided under the Bill. 
Purifying sea water into drinking water 
2453. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware of the fact that certain State Government 
have set up plants in rural areas to convert sea water into protected drinking 
water; 
(b) if so, whether any action plan has been taken to finance those plants by 
giving suitable assistance to State Government; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL. 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) and (b) Some of the State 
Governments have setup plants in rural areas to convert sea water into protected 
drinking water. As rural drinking water supply is a State subject and Government 
of India provides financia l and technical assistance to States to accelerate 
coverage of rural habitations through a centrally sponsored scheme, namely 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP), action plans to set-up 
and finance these plants are drawn up by the State Governments. 
(c) and (d) 15% of ARWSP funds allocated to the State Governments are 
earmarked for tackling quality problems, including salinity, by setting up 
desalination plants both for brackish water and conversion of sea water into potable 
water. The funding pattern between the Centre and the States is in the ratio of 
75:25. Full powers have been delegated to the State Governments for 
sanctioning and implementing projects for tackling quality problems.

Misappropriation of funds for rural development programmes by 
NGOs 
2456. SHRI JANARDHAN A POOJARY: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a number of NGOs are blacklisted for 
misappropriation of funds extended for undertaking various rural development 
programmes; 
(b) if so, what are the details, within quantum of funds sanctioned and 
accounted for during the last three years, year-wise and State-wise; 
(c) whether any inquiry has been initiated for fixing responsibility for 
indiscreet sanctions and action taken against defaulting NGOs and for 
recovery of the sanctioned amount; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The names and addresses of the organizations blacklisted, amount 
sanctioned and released, State-wise and year-wise during the last three years, are 
given in the enclosed Statement (see below). 
(c) Yes, Sir. The projects sanctioned to the NGOs are periodically 
monitored to ensure percolation of bene fits to the intended beneficiaries and 
proper utilization of grant in aid released to them. Defaulting NGOs are given 
opportunities to rectify mistakes committed, failing which, such NGOs are 
blacklisted. FIRs are filed against them for recovery of misutilised funds. 
(d) During the last three years, CAPART has blacklisted 66 NGOs for 
committing various irregularities, out of which 35 NGOs have been 
blacklisted during the year 2004-05 only (till 15th March, 2005) for 
submitting forged documents. 30 out of 35 NGOs have not received any fund 
from CAPART. FIRs have been filed against erring organisations and its 
functionaries at the concerned Police Stations.

Survey for identifying BPL families 
2460. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: W ill the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has conducted any State-wise survey to identify facilities 
available to Below Poverty Line families in the country; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details thereof; and

families in different States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) to (c) The Ministry of 
Rural Development have not conducted any State-wise survey to identify facilities available 
to Below Poverty Line families in the country. However, the Ministry provides assistance 
to the States/UTs to conduct a BPL Census to identify the BPL families in the rural areas 
who could be provided assistance under different programmes of the Ministry. The 
Ministry is implementing two major poverty alleviation programmes namely, 
Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) to provide wage-employment, Swarnjayanti 
Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) to provide self-employment through bank credit and 
subsidy. The Government has also recently launched a National Food For Work 
Programme (NFFWP) in 150 most backward districts in the country with the objective 
to provide additional employment opportunities to the rural poor. Under Indira Awaas 
Yojana (IAY) the rural poor are provided assistance to built houses. In addition, the 
Ministry is also implementing Rural Drinking Water Supply and Rural Sanitation 
Schemes to improve the quality of life of the rural poor. Under the Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) roads are constructed to improve the rural 
connectivity.

potentially viable textile units having debt exposure of Rs. 2 crore 
and above; 
(v) De-reservation of the woven segment of readymade garments from 
the SSI sector. In the Union Budget 2005-06, an announcement has 
been made for de-resevation of 30 hosiery items from the ambit of 
SSI; 
(vi) Launching of "Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting 
focused thrust for setting up of apparel manufacturing units of 
international standards at potential growth centres and to give fillip 
to exports; 
(vii) Launching of "Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" 
(TCIDS) for upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile 
centres; 
(viiii) Launching of "Cotton Technology Mission" to improve the 
productivity and quality of cotton;

2470. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Commission for Women in its study report has 
indicated that the financial position of Bhadohi carpet weavers, 70 per cent of which 
constitute women, is precarious and it will further worsen unless Government help is 
rendered to extricate them out of poverty; and 
(b) if so, the problems in brief faced by these weavers and Government's action plan to 
help them out? 
12.00 Noon 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) and (b) On 
the basis of the observations and recommendation made in the 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [23 March, 2005] 
Public Hearing of Women in Carpet Industry held on 5.8.2004 at Bhodohi, Uttar 
Pradesh, the National Commission for Women (NCW) has reported that the 
proportion of women in the carpet weaving craft is 30 per cent and the condition 
of women weavers is precarious and needs Government help. 
As per the report of NCW the problems faced by Women Carpet Weavers include: 
lack of social security; lack of awareness of Government schemes; exploitation by 
private traders; no schools for girls near their Villages beyond class-V; lack of 
drinking water and health facilities. 
The State Government of Uttar Pradesh has been requested to take steps to 
solve the problems related to drinking water, health etc. The Carpet Export 
Promotion Council (CEPC) and All India Carpet Manufacturing Association, 
Bhadohi have bee advised to ensure compliance as per law provisions.

Demand to Formulate Gu jarat Coastal and Border Area Management 
Plan and separate Marine Police Wing 
SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI (Gujarat): Sir, Gujarat has a coastal line of 1640 
kms. In order to provide adequate secu rity for the coastal areas, a Coastal 
Security Plan for Rs.392 crores was submitted to the Government of India. 
We suggest that the Navy and Coast Guard should be made solely 
responsible for patrolling of the high seas and the coastal security of the territorial 
waters of Gujarat. Though it is a fact that the prime responsibility of ensuring 
complete maritime security lies with the Indian Coast Guard, which cannot be 
ignored or diluted, the pr esent proposal incorporat es the role of State 
Police,however, limited in nature, which can only be as supplementary 
assistance to the existing coastal security. There are a number of creeks and 
uninhabited islands, very close to Gujarat, towards Pakistan side. These creeks 
and islands may become a safe haven for infiltrators, smugglers etc. for anti-
national activities. It is, therefore, requested that the Government of India should 
make appropriate addition to the present coastal security set up of Navy and the 
Coast Guard, and also consider setting up of separate marine police wing in 
each coastal police station, which should be properly equipped and trained.

Demand to tackle and control tuberculosis and Malaria in 
Jharkhand 
SHRI R.K. ANAND (Jharkhand): Sir, it is really awesome that even after more 
than five decades of our Independence, diseases like TB and Malaria are spreading 
and taking their toll in the country. It is estimated that more than four lakh patients 
die of TB every year in the country. Today Malaria cases are around 2 to 3 million 
a year. The situation in the newly-creat ed State of Jharkhand is more serious. 
Most of the inhabitants are tribals and workers of various mines, mainly coal 
mines. Due to poverty leading to malnutrition has resulted in rising TB cases in 
the State. During 2000 to September, 2002, as many as 178 TB patients died due 
to this disease in the State. During the same period 68 people lost their lives due to 
Malaria. Cases of other vector-borne diseases like Dengue, Kala Azar and Japanese 
Encephalitis and Filariasis are also ra mpant. The Government on its parts is 
implementing DOTS as WHO recommended strategy to control TB but coverage 
has to be rapidly increased in the State. Central assistance is needed for 
establishing more and more diagnostic centres in the State so that TB cases are 
diagnosed well in time to start right treatment under DOTS. 
Malaria is a local and focal problem in the State. It turns epidemic during the 
summer and rainy seasons. To reduce the malaria cases, mosquitoes need to 
be eliminated. Diagnostic centres need to be incresed. The people in tribal and 
village areas need to be supplied with adequate supplies of approved 
insecticides and larvicides, medicated bed nets for personal protection apart from 
adequate quantities of anti-malaria drugs through village level health centres. In 
this, village panchayats can also be involved. Information campaigns also needed 
to be launched.

procedure is that as soon as the Bill is passed by the other House, it is transmitted to this

the Bill be taken into consideration. The actual date of consideration comes after 
giving two days' notice. But under Rule 123, the Chairman has been authorised to 
give direction, and we have sought his permission because of the urgency of the 
Bill. The hon. Member herself has admitted that this is an Ordinance and the Bill

and approval. The reason why we have to do it is that this leg of the Session will

commencement of the Session i.e. on the 8th April. This Ordinance is related to

amendment; now, this is the third amendment. I occupied that seat which my

1999, the hon. Members who are sitting in the Opposition now, were in the

be defined as a basic novel product, or, process involving inventive step and capable of 
industrial application and not as has been explained in Section 2 of the Act. As the hon. 
Minister is aware, the WTO is yet to complete its mandated review of life forms. So, I suggest

mailbox applications. For example, there are nearly 7000 applications received in

minor changes to the structure of molecules. So, I strongly plead for grant of

to fight with the strong multinational companies.

this Bill to a Joint Select  Committee. Let it go to a Joint Select Committee. I 
request for sending the Bill to the Joint Select Committee or, the concerned

Statement 
(a) to (c) Indian bio-tech industry has made considerable progress in last 
half decade. As per the BioSpectru m-ABLE (Association of Biotechnology-
Led Enterprises) survey of Indian Biotech Industry, the number of companies in 
the Biotechnology Sector has grown to 235 in the year 2003-2004 as compared to 
about 150 in the previous year. Indian Biotech sector has obtained critical 
mass in manufacturing as well as research services and has slowly built a 
market for biotech products and services estimated at $700 million for the Year 
2003-2004 and is well on its way to reach its targeted $1 billion market size by 
2005 and $5 billion by 2010 (Estimate by ABLE). Indian Biotechnol ogy is 
now poised to leverage its scientific skills and technical experience to make a 
global impact on a strong innovation led platform. 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005]

sector with an impetus for the development and promotion by providing 
incentives like: reduction in custom duty on specified machinery; 150 percent 
weighted deduction on in-house R&D e xpenditure; equity support to small 
and medium enterprises through Small Industries Development. Bank of India 
(SIDBI). Under the Foreign Trade Policy 2004-09, all benefits enjoyed by Export 
Oriented Units (EOU) have been passed on to Biotech Parks (BTP) in the country

through Automatic Route similar to Special Economic Zones (SEZ) untis. BTP 
units are exempted from payment of Income Tax as per the provisions of Section 
10A & 10B of the IT Act.

formulated their state specific biotech policies and established biotech parks to 
boost the biotechnology sector in their respective states and the Department of 
Biotechnology (DBT), GOI is contributing to their effort by supporting creation 
of incubator/pilot level facilities in these parks.

Master level and Ph. D. programmes to meet industry demand apart from 
strengthening of infrastructure in the university systems and research 
institutes.

Capability of ports for modern vessels 
*332. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Country's ports are capable of handling new generation 
vessels; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the steps taken by Government to make these ports capable of 
handling new generation vessels? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (c) Lack of globally comparable port 
infrastructure, mainly, inadequate depth in port channels and basins and cargo 
handling facilities which include berths, terminals, cargo handling equipments, 
etc. limit the capacity of Indian ports to handle new generation vessels. It is not, 
however, economically prudent to make investments in creating infrastructure for 
handling new generation vessels for all commodity categories in all the ports. 
Creation of infrastructure in the major ports depends on the present cargo mix 
in these ports, future traffic potential for various categories of cargo, assessment of 
the categories of vessels which may call at these ports, etc, after taking into 
account the demands of maritime trade. This is an on-going process. As part of 
this process, major ports undertake capital dredging for deepening of port basins and 
channels from time to time to keep pace with the draught requirements of 
vessels calling at these ports, construct new berths, expand existing berths and 
also acquire/upgrade their cargo handling equipment.

2510. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS

(b) whether any structural deficiencies in  the Act or lack of foresight of

raising questions about India's data-protection laws, etc. at that point of time

etc. are taken into confidence by the Expert Panel? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) The 
terms of reference of the Expert Panel set up to review the Information 
Technology Act, 2000 are given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
The main objective of the IT Act, 2000 is to promote Electronic Commerce and 
Electronic Governance through the enabling legislation to legally recognise 
the electronic media as equivalent of paper based system including cyber 
security, data protection and cyber crimes. 
Electronic Commerce and Electronic Govemnance are on-going evolution and as 
a result of fast developments, there is need to continuously 
88 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
harmonise the entire infrastructure and statutes with the changing 
requirements. 
The IT Act 2000 is based on the Model Law prepared by United Nation's 
Commission on International Trade and Laws (UNCITRAL) of January 1997. 
However, for reasons explained above, UNCITRAL came up with revised Model 
Law in December 2001. Further the September 11 episode of the World Trade 
Center New York posed certain challeng es for the cyber security and a re-
look was felt essential. In additional there are several other technological 
developments taken place due to convergence of computers, communications 
and content and it is therefore necessary to examine their impact on the 
legislation, if any. 
Therefore, Department of Information Technology has set up the Expert Panel 
to re-examine the Information Technology Act, 2000 in the light of the above 
issues. 
(b) The IT Act 2000 is based on the Model Law prepared by United 
Nation's Commission on International Trade and Laws (UNCITRAL) of 
January 1997. Therefore, the Act had taken tino accont all the relevant 
issues including the international inputs at that point in time. 
The Expert Panel would go into the details of changes or new legislation required 
to curb the cyber crimes under the IT Act or any other laws of the land. 
The matter of data protection being raised by the off-shoring clients, 
especially by those from the member countries of European Union (EU) is also 
one the terms of reference of the Expert Panel. 
(c) The Expert Panel already has ad equate representation of relevant 
associations, industry experts and the law professionals. Any other 
consultations required would also be carried out appropriately. 
Statement 
Terms of reference of Expert Panel to review Information Technology 
Act 2000 
1. To re-exaine the IT Act, 2000 so as to ensure that the Act remains enabler 
to development of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) 
and has adequate measures for promoting growth

of electronic commerce a nd electronic governance in  the country and 
also for regulating cyber crimes and cyber forensics as well as addresses 
all aspects of the cyber security etc.  in a manner that there is no socpe 
for different interpretations and follo ws the international guidelines for 
uniformity to gain from the process of globalisation. 
2. To consider the recommendations made by the Inter-Ministerial 
Working Group on Cyber Law & Cyber Forensics & finalize the 
amendments to the IT Act, 2000. 
3. To consider and recommend suitable legislation for data protection 
(Privacy) in the IT Act, 2000. 
4. To consider the feability of making IT Act, 2000 technology neutral and

2616. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minsiter of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state:

2531. SHRI DATTAMEGHE: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether President George W. Bush has signed into law a bill that binds the 
United States to a long term commitment to support Pakistan; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI RAO 
INDERJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. President Bush signed the "Intelligence Reform and 
Terrorism Preventbn Act of 2004" on December 17,2004. Section 7103 of the Act provides the 
legislative basis for a long-term U.S. policy to Pakistan. It conveys U.S. concerns in 
regard to that country, reflects U.S. assessments about certain critical issues, and spells out 
U.S. objectives vis-a-vis Pakistan and the larger region. Section 7103 of the Act 
contemplates: 
* A deeper and longer-term commitment by the United States to Pakistan, 
including maintenance of present levels of aid. 
* A two-year waiver to Pakistan from various legislative provisions restricting 
aid, covering FY 2005 and FY 2006. 
* An internal reform thrust in Pakistan, focusing on its educational system and 
governance process, particularly in regard to tribal areas. 
* Addressing Pakistani concerns, including outstanding difficulties with its 
neighbours and other countries in the region. 
(c) Government of India understands U.S. efforts in addressing the socio-economic, 
proliferation and terrorism-linked concerns emanating from Pakistan. Government's 
strong concerns on U.S. military assistance to Pakistan, however, have been conveyed to 
the U.S. Government.

(c) the benefits, if any, derived by studies carried out; and 
131

(d) the details of fund allocated/expe nses incurred on the COMAPS since 
its launching, year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes Sir, the Coastal Ocean 
Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) was launched during the year 
1991-92 to collect data on the levels of Marine Pollutants in the Coastal 
waters of the country. 
(b) The main objective of the progr amme is to analyse the trend of 
decrease/increase of pollutants in the coasal waters of major cities, towns and 
other locations of industrial importance. Collection of data on 25 pollution 
and other related parameters (such as Biochemical Oxygen Demand, 
pathogenic bacteria, toxic metals like cadmium, mercury and lead in 
sediments) at 72-80 locations was carried out with the help of the following 
institutions; 
(i) National Institute of Oceanography, Goa and its Regional Centres at Kochi, 
Mumbai and Visakhapatnam 
(ii) Regional Centre, Central Electro Chemical Research Institute, Chennai 
and Tuticorin/Annamalai University 
(iii) Regional Research Laboratory, Bhubaneswar 
(iv) Centre for Earth Science Studies, Thiruvananthapuram and Zonal Office, 
Central Pollution Control Board, Kolkata 
(v) Andaman and Nicobar Centre for Ocean Science & Technology, 
National Institute of Ocean Technology, Port Blair 
• The Annamalai University/Anna Un iversity and DOD's Integrated 
Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) Project Directorate have 
been entrusted with the task of monitoring of pesticides like Dichloro-
diphenyl-trichloroethane(DDT), Hexachloro-cyclo-hexane (HCH) and 
Endosulfan in edible fish and bivalves. 
• The Regional Research Laboratory, Thiruvananthapuram was entrusted 
with the responsibility of cunducting inter calibration exercises to 
confirm the data quality 
• The task on development of GIS database has been entrusted to (I) 
132 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Institute for Ocean Management, Anna University (ii) ICMAM Project Directorate of 
the Department of Ocean Development 
• The National Institute of Ocean Technology has been entrusted with 
the task of modelling studies to understand the diffusion and 
dispersion characteristics of pollutants. 
(c) As a result of the systematic monitoring of the coastal areas, health of our seas 
could be assessed and areas of low medium and high concentrations of pollutants 
could be identified. The areas of high concentration of pollutants are being monitored 
intensively. Details of these locations are: 
• Areas of clean sea water quality: 
The sea approx. beyond 1 km. along the coastline of India except off Bombay is clean 
and conforms to quality of clean water. In Bombay' the sea off 5 km is clean. This is 
primarily due to the fact that the levels of dissolved oxygen-and other parameters fulfill 
the requirements of clean sea water. 
• Areas of no concern: 
In Vadinar and Kandla of Gujarat, Ratnagiri in Maharashtra, Mandovi and Zuari in 
Goa, Mangalore Port in Karnataka, Cannanore and Calicut in Kerala, Cuddalore in Tamil 
Nadu and the West Bengal Coast, the concentrations of dissolved oxygen was fairly good 
and other toxic elements like ammoma, heavy metals in sediments and biota were slightly 
higher (about 15%) than the clean waters. 
• Areas that need intensive monitoring: 
In Porbondar, Bamanganga estuary, and Vapi industrial estate in Gujarat, 
Mangalore coast in Karnataka, Kochi backwaters, Quilon, Paravur in Kerala and Tuticorin 
and Arumuganeri in Tamil Nadu, Puri in Orissa the levels of dissolved oxygen were 
moderate to normal and however some of the elements like ammonia, pathogenic 
bacteria in sea water and heavy metals in sediments showed higher concentration (about 
25%) then the normal values. Due to the definite source of pollutants chances of increase 
in concentration are likely to be high, these areas need intensive monitoring. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
Areas on concern: 
In Veraval Port in Gujarat, Versova Creek, Mahim Bay and Thane Creek in 
Maharashtra, Veli in Kerala, Visakha patnam Harbout and Kakinada Bay 
(canal) in Andhra Pradesh, the concentrations of dissolved oxygen were nil to 
low during low tide period and improved their levels only moderately (30-
50%) during the high tide period. Further, the levels of toxic metals like 
cadmium and level were high in sediments in some locations (like Thane 
Creek) and pH was very low (Veli). If no control measures are exercised now, 
the areas will become regions of high c oncentrations of pollution in another 5 
to 6 years. 
Levels of organochlorine pesticides like HCH and DDT were analysed in 32 
species of marine fish collected at various locations along the east coast of India. 
The levels of both the chemicals were very much lower than those observed in the 
terrestrial animals and other food items. These levels are well below the limits (5 
parts/billion is the safety limit) set by the Health authorities. This would 
indicate that the marine fish is not contaminated with the pesticide residues in 
the locations from which the samples were collected.

(a) the number of families related to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled

Tribes/Other Backward Classes and weaker section of society living below poverty

(b) whether the number of such families have increased during the last three 
years;

(d) the details of the steps being take n for upliftment of these weaker 
families? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Planning Commission does not estimate the number 
of families living below the Poverty Line in the country. However, it estimates 
poverty at national and state level from the large sample survey on Household 
Consumer Expenditure conducted by the National Sample Organisation (NSSO) 
at an interval of approximately five years. The latest such survey was conducted in 
1999-2000 (NSS 55th Round). On the basis of this Household Consumer 
Expenditure Survey, the percentage of SC/ ST persons living Below Poverty Line 
in 1999-2000 for the major states in enclosed as Statement (See below). The 
corresponding data for Other Backward Classes and weaker sections of 
society are separately not available. 
(b) and (c) The most recent NSSO  data on House hold Consumption 
Expenditure is available only for 1999-2000. As such the data for the last three 
years are not available. 
(d) The Government has taken three pronged strategy of Social 
Empowerment, Economic Empowerment and Social Justice, with an ultimate 
aim to fulfil the Constitutional commitment of raising the status of the Scheduled 
Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes at par with the rest of the 
society. The approach adopted to empower these groups is to achieve overall 
improvement in their socio-economic status through attending to their special 
problems and needs. 
Economic empowerment of these weaker sections of SCs/OBCs and 
Minorities has always been accorded priority especia lly focusing poverty 
alleviation through promoting employment and income generating activities. To this 
effect, various employment-cum-income generation activities are being 
implemented with the objective of making these disadvantaged groups economically 
independent and self-reliant. Towards promoting economic 
154 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
development amongst SCs and STs, Special Central Assistances (SCA) to Special 
Component Plan (SCP) and Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) are being extended to states/UTs on 
the basis of their popultion and relative backwardness. Special efforts are also being 
made through National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation 
(NSCFDC), State SC Development Corporations (SCDCs), National Safai Karamchari 
Finance & Development Corporation (NSKFDC), National Scheduled Tribes Finance & 
Development Corporation (NSTFDC), National Backward Classes Finance and Development 
Corporation (NBCFDC) and National Minorities Development and Finance Corporation 
(NMDFC) for economic development of these socially disadvantaged groups. These 
Corporations also provide skill and entrepreneurial training to unemployed youth through 
reputed training institutions. 
Besides, for poverty alleviation in rural areas, the Ministry of Rural Development is 
implementing two programmes i.e. Sampobrna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) and 
Swamjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) a wage employment and self-employment 
programmes respectively. By these two programmes SC/ST families are also benefited. 
During 2003-04, at national level 8560.24 lakh mandays of employment were generated, of 
which 2827.23 lakh mandays were generated for scheduled castes and 2025.03 lakh mandays 
were generated for scheduled tribes respectively, under self-employment programme, SGSY, 
during 2003-04 the total number of Swarozgaris assisted at national level was 896424 of which 
275186 no. of Swarozgaris were from scheduled castes communities and 13821 no. of 
Swarozgaris were from scheduled tribes communities. 
In urban areas, the Ministry of Urban Employments Poverty Alleviation is implementing 
a Centrally Sponsored urban poverty alleviation programme called Swarna Jayanti Shahari 
Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) through all the States/UTs w.e.f. 1.12.1997. Under the 
Urban, Self-Employment Programme (USEP) component of this scheme urban unemployed 
or underemployed poor living below the poverty line are encouraged to set up self-
employment ventures relating to servicing, petty business and manufacturing 
units. There are no minimum educational qualifications for the beneficiaries under this 
scheme. However, scheme is not applicable to the beneficiaries educated beyond the IX 
standard. There is a special sub-component under USEP component of SJSRY called 
Development of Women and Child in Urban Areas (DWCUA), which is intended for urban

poor women only for facilitating them to set up employment ventures in groups. A 
DWCUA group is minimum of 10 urban poor women. During 2003-04,19884 no. of 
Scheduled Castes people under USEP (subsidy) sub-component, and 8494 no. of Scheduled 
Castes people under DWCUA groups were assisted to set up self-employment ventures 
under Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana.

waive off the Central Debt;

M.V. RAJASEKHARAN). (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. Several State 
157

governments have sought debt write-off. Details are indicated in the enclosed Statement (See 
below). 
Government of India is generally guided by the recommendations of the Finance 
Commission is not generally agreed to. Twelfth Finance Commission has 
recommended consolidation and reschedulement of Government of India loans to State 
Governments for a fesh period of 20 years at 7.5% rate of interest of States which adopt 
fiscal responsibility legislation as per the recommendations of the Finance Commission. 
The Twelfth Finance Commission has recommended a debt write-off scheme linked 
to reduction in revenue deficit by States. The quantum of write-off of repayment would be

this recommendation, the benefit of write-off would be available only if the fiscal deficit 
of the State is contained to the level of 2004-05. If in any year, the fiscal deficit exceeds this 
level, the benefit of write-off, even if eligible otherwise, would not be given. States 
are likely to get waiver of Rs. 32198.69 crores over the period 2005-2010, if they meet 
all conditions of the scheme.

2591. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is large scale exodus of scientists from India to foreign 
countries in search of better career options; 
(b) whether such migration of top scientists from reputed institutes and organisations in 
the Country is on account of inadequate pay and perks, lack of career options and 
poor working conditions; 
(c) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(d) the measures that are proposed to be taken to encourage the scientists to stay 
behind and contribute to the development of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) to (c) Some scientists do migrate to other 
countries for various reasons including financial and academic gains. However, no 
record of such scientists leaving the country is being maintained centrally. 
(d) Several measures have been taken from time to time by the Government to 
minimize the outflow and to contribute to the development of the country. Some of 
these measures are: 
Setting up of centres of excellence/advanced studies in the universities 
and academic institutions. 
Creation of core groups of professionals with necessary modem facilities required 
for pursuing research in new and frontier areas of science. 
S&T based training for enterpreneurial development. 
Increase in the outlay for science and technology sector in successive Five Year Plan. 
Creation of new scientific Departments/Organisations. 
Delegation of advanced administrative and financial powers to S&T institutions to 
improve working conditions of scientists. 
Manpower development training/re.training programmes through 
associateships/fellowships.

Fast Track Scheme for Young Scientists.

High Berthing Charges in Shipping Industry 
2603. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the high berthing charges are acting as a negative point in 
increased shipping activity in the country; 
(b) the guideline issued by Government to various port trusts in this regard to 
maintain a competitive set of berthing charges; 
(c) whether Government would take steps to bring down the present rates charged 
by all major port trusts in the country; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that inefficiency and high port charges are suffocating 
the entire shipping industry; and 
(e) the steps proposed to study such hindrances being caused to the development of 
the shipping sector in the country? 
184 

 
[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T. R. BAALU): (a) and (d) Increased shipping activity inter-alia is 
dependent upon growing exim trade, tax regime, availablity to finance for 
purchase of vessels etc. The berthing charges perse are not acting as a negative 
point in increased shipping adtivity in the country. 
(b), (c) and (e) The Port Tariffs and scale of rates in major ports is fixed by an 
autonomous Authority viz. Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) which was 
constituted in April, 1997 under the Major Port Trust Act, 1963. The tariffs fixed 
by TAMP are ceiling rates. However, Ports have the flexibility to charge tariffs 
below the ceiling rates. TAMP is presently following cost plus approach for 
fixing tariff. Endeavour of the Government is to explore if cost plus approach can 
gradually be replaced by normative a pproach. The TAMP has constituted a 
Working Group on normative cost based tariff for container related charges.

Modernising of office of DG-Shipping 
2614. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any effort is being made to modernise the office of the Director 
General of Shipping; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the same systems are in place as fifty years ago; 
(c) whether Government have done any study on how to convert the office of DG 
(Shipping) from a purely regulatory body into one which is also development-
oriented; 
(d) the steps that would be taken to open up the office and simplify the rules and 
procedures; and 
(e) the details of steps proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI 
T.R. BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) No, Sir. The office of Director General of Shipping has undergone change to keep 
pace with the development in maritime sector. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) and (e) the following steps have been taken to open up office of DG (Shipping) and 
relax/simplify the rules and procedures:— 
(i) Relaxation in provisions of 407(1) of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 allowing 
movement of containers by foreign ships between Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (NJPT), 
Mumbai to any other port in India or vice-versa and development of cruise shipping 
industry in India; 
(ii) 50% fee concession and age relaxation allowed for women in maritime training; 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
(iii) more than 125 maritime Training Institutes opened in private sector in 
different parts of the country; 
(iv) continuous up-dation of Maritime Laws to keep pacewith requirements of the 
International Conventions and our shipping industry; 
(v) Tonnage-tax regime has been introduced with effect from 01.01.2005 which 
has resulted in increase in Indian tonnage; 
(vi) Computerization of the Directorate and its allied offices; 
(vii) Indian Database of Seafarers (INDoS) has been set up at the Lal 
Bahadur Shastri College of Advanced martitime Studies and Research, 
with a view to cater to the verification of certificates and documents 
possessed by seafarers; 
(viii) The examination centres at Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai have been 
modernised to ensure that all training and certification is carried out under 
a quality system duly certified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) 
(ix) An additional examination centre at NOIDA near New Delhi, has been 
opened to accommodate the seafarers from the northern parts of the 
country; 
(x) All important Acts, rules orders and circulars issued by DG(S) are 
available on its web site. 
Production of traditional items by MNCs 
2615. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that MNCs have also ventured into manufacturing things 
that have been traditionally undertaken by small scale industries; 
(b) If so, whether Government have ascertained the extent to which the small 
scale industries suffer due to this competition from MNCs; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to provide competitive edge to SSI units? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) As per the notification issued by the Central Government in 
204 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
December 1997, in exercise of the powers conferre d under the Industries 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 industries which are not small scale 
industries (SSIs), including MNCs, can manufacture items reserved for exclusive 
manufacture by the SSI on the condition that 50 per cent of their production 
would be exported. 
(b) No specific study has been conducted to ascertain the extent to which 
the small scale industries might have been affected due to competition from 
MNCs. However, from the fact that the annual rate of growth of production of 
the SSI sector has so far been consistently higher than that of the country's 
industrial sector as a whole, it can be inferred that the SSI sector has generally 
been able to face up to the competition in the market, including that from the 
MNCs. 
(c) To enhance the competitiveness of the SSI units, the Government have 
put in place a slow of measures, whic h include assistance for technological 
upgradation, accessing markets, improved infrastructure, better availability of 
credit, facilities for training and capacity building of entrepreneurs,etc. 
Closure of SSI units 
2616. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of SMALL    • 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of SSI units closed down during the past three years; 
(b) the reasons for such closure; and 
(c) the steps taken or to be taken to give filling to revival of SSI in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) As per the latest information available with the Government based 
on the Third All India Census of the Small Scale Industries with reference to 
the year 2001-02, 8,87,427 registered units were found closed. 
(b) Apart from voluntary closure of SSI units, the main reasons of closure are 
inadequacy/shortage of working capital, fall in demand, changes in 
technology, shortage of raw materials, marketing problems, increase in 
competition, management inadequacies, etc.    
205 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
(c) Although the promotion and development of Small Scale Industries is primarily the 
responsibility of the State/Union Territory (UT) Governments/ Administrations, the Central 
Government assists and supplements these efforts. For revival of sick small scale 
industries, the State and Central Governments have taken steps like establishing institution. 
I forums in the form of State-Level Inter-Institutional Committee and Distrct-Level sick 
Units Rehabilitation Committees in some States for periodical review, special 
rehabilitation cells in banks and State financial institutions, national level committee for 
improving credit flow, etc. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued guidelines on 16 
January, 2002 for rehabilitation of sick SSI units, which include modification in the 
definition of sick SSI units, norms for deciding their viability, several measures to extend 
concessional finance for reviving potentially viable sick SSI units, etc. 
SSIs in Jammu & Kashmir 
2617. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that terrorists activities in Jammu and Kashmir have adversely 
affected the small scale industries there; 
(b) the steps Government propose to take to put on rail the strife SSI in J&K 
(c) the total amount of funds allocated for development of SSI for the year 2005-06 
and the share allocated for J&K; and 
(d) the details of small scale industries in J & K likely to benefit from the allocation 
for the year 2005-06? 
THE MINISTER SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) Sir, the Government of Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) has reported in 
the affirmative. 
(b) The Central Government announced a new industrial policy and other 
concessions for J&K in June, 2002. This policy, inter alia, included enhanced central 
grant (upto Rs. 4 crore) for setting up of Integrated Infrastructure Development (IID) 
Centre, 100 percent Central excise duty exemption to the new units located in notified 
areas and for substantial expansion by the existing, investment subsidy at the rate of 15 
per cent 
206 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of investment in plant and machinery subject to a ceiling of Rs. 30 lakh, interest subsidy 
of 3 per cent on working capital loans to new units in notified locations, etc., The State 
Government also announced its new industrial policy in 2004 and provided various 
incentives to industrial units. 
(c) An amount of Rs. 412.26 crore has been provisionally allocated in the Plan budget of 
the Central Government for various schemes of assistance to SSI units for the year 2005-06. 
The allocation of these funds is made scheme-wise and not State-wise. 
(d) The schemes/programmes of the Central Government supplement the efforts of the 
States/Union Territories for promotion of small scale industries so as to create an 
environment conducive for the entrepreneurs to establish industries in the small scale 
sector. The State Government has informed that 2758 units have been established in 
J&K, after the announcement of the new industrial policy by the Central Government in 
2002 and the State Government in 2004.

' Request for Honouring Freedom Fighter, Shri Pingali Venkaiah 
SHRI K. RAMAMOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, Pingali Venkaiah, 
Gandhian, the creator of our nation 's tricolour that gave enthusiasm, 
exuberance and patriotism to our country men in achieving our independence, 
died in poverty, in a small hut near Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh. His only and 
the ultimate dream was to look at National Flag, designed by him, fluttering at 
the ramparts of Red Fort. But the most piti able thing is, neither he could afford to 
go himself nor his family members could afford to take him to Delhi to see his 
National Flag flying from the Red Fort. 
231

He died in a pitiable condition. Is this the recognition we are giving to a great freedom 
fighter? He met Mahatma Gandhi in south Africa, and since then had a very close assocation 
with him. Our beloved leader had put up a statue of this pat riot on Tank Bund, 
Hyderabad. 
The most astonishing thing is that the Government of India has neither sanctioned any 
freedom fighters' pension nor any other benefit to his family members. The only known 
survivor of his family is his dauthter who is earning her livelihood by selling papads 
and pickles. I request the Government of India to immediately sanction pension to the family 
members of the architect of the Tricolour, and a lession on him should be introduced in the 
curriculum of the textbooks depicting his life history. I request for converting his house into 
a memorial, and it should be handed over to the ASI for its maintenance. I also request for 
release of a postal stamp which is a befitting tribute to the great soul.

Demand for adequate compensation to the fishermen families in all Tsunami-

SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, during the recent Tsunami, 
1000 kms of coastal areas of Tamil Nadu and Pondicherry and nine lakhs of families had been

Nicobar Island were also very badly affected due to Tsunami and earthquake. In 
Andaman alone, the total estimated loss is about Rs. 3000 crores and more than 5000

only Rs. 10,000 is given as compensation which is too meagre to reconstruct the houses. 
Though 10,000 persons were declared dead and missing officially, the real death toll is over 
30,000, as claimed by the Red Cross. The Nicobar Island is worst affected where, apart from 
the tribals of that area, the non-tribals numbering more

Demand for allocation of more Central funds to combat aids in 
Tamil Nadu 
SHRI S. ANBALAGAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, a steep increase in HIV-positive cases 
continues to cause serious concern in the country. This calls for urgent efforts at the 
national level to eradicate AIDS. An estimate shows that 51 lakh men, women and 
children in the country have been affected with HIV/AIDS, by the end of 2003. The 
States of Nagaland and Tamil Nadu have been categorised as high-prevalence 
States. About 14 other States have been categorised as highly vulnerable States. 
So, I request the Government to pay more attention to HIV infection in the country. The 
National Council of AIDS, headed by the hon. Prime Minister, should make all-out 
efforts to end this m enace. Tamil Nadu being a high prevalence State, the State 
Government of Tamil Nadu has taken several steps to control AIDS. The Union 
Government should render more assistance to the States and provide infrastructural 
facilities to fight the disease. More Government hospitals, particularly, in Tamil Nadu 
should be equipped to provide anti-retroviral treatment to HIV affected persons. 
Assistance should also be rendered by the Union Government for opening more 
community care centres in the State, for the promotion of community home-based 
care for HIV positive persons. I have come to know that the Naitonal AIDS 
Research Institute in Pune has developed a vaccine to prevent AIDS. I urge upon the 
Government to expedite human clinical trials of the vaccine. I also urge the 
Government to make continuous research till an effective vaccine is invented to 
prevent AIDS. 
SHRI N.R. GOVINDRAJAR (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I associated myself with the 
Special Mention made by the hon. Member. 
Demand for solar-power fencing in agricultural lands to protect the crops 
from the wild animals 
SHRI N.R. GOVINDRAJAR (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to bring to the notice of the 
august House and to the Government the hardships being faced by the farmers of 
Tamil Nadu, particularly in the areas of Gobichettipalayam constituency, that is 
Sathyamangalam, Anthiyur and Ammapettai to which I belong. There is no doubt 
that economic development counts for the development of a nation; however, 
agricultural development is the foremost for the development of any nation. The 
hardships the farmer faces in bringing up his crops are countless. He has to wait for 
the monsoon, took for loans from the Government and private institution, work in 
field along with his 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
whole family. There is a saying in Tamil which means "breaking the pot while 
churning for the butter". Similarly while waiting for the harvest, the farmers in 
these areas face the threat of wild animals like elephants and boars damaging the 
crops in the night, and thereby resulting in great loss to the farmers and affecting the 
farmers' whole family. I, therefore, urge the Government to come out with a scheme 
with subsidy for solar-power fencing through Non-Conventional Energy Resources as 
in the case of subsidy for agricultural inputs and streetlights through non-conventional 
energy resources. I am sure such schemes would definitely help the farmers to 
establish solar-power fences in their agricultural lands to protect their crops from 
the wild animals as well as to save their lives. Thank you. 
SHRI S. ANBALAGAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I associate myself with the Special

Demand to bring a suitable legislation to safeguard the right to 
gender equality 
SHRIMAT IS.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, it is necessary to enact suitable 
legislation to safeguard, preserve and enforcement of the right to gender equality 
of the working women. It has been reported that in so many incidents, female sections 
have been sexually harassed by higher, senior male officials as a tradeoff for declaring 
them fit for commissiong as officers and promotion. Not only for promotion, there are so 
many reasons where the female sections are suffering in so many ways, which cannot 
be expressed. It is the duty of the employer to safeguard the female employee and 
he is the responsible person to take steps for the prosecution of the accused and to 
take preventive steps. He has to take disciplinary action and to form the 
compliance committee headed by a woman and not less than half of its members 
should be women which is helpful for the affected women to initiate complaints and 
get remedy. There is no specific law in this regard. So, I appeal to the 
Government to take suitable measures  including legislation to ensure the 
protection of the working women in all sector. Thank you. 
Need to set up a National Judicial Commission 
SHRI VI JAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): I would like to draw the attention of this 
House to the urgent matter of public importance on setting up a National 
Judicial Commission. 
Sir, legal fraternity and enlightened public have been asking for setting up of a 
National Commission for making appointment of High Court Judges 
236 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
determining their service conditions, drawing up code of ethics, probity, transfers, etc. There 
has been serious erosion of faith in the judicial system in general public and growing suspicion 
in the integrity of higher judiciary. Presently, the Supreme Court has neither administrative 
control over the High Court Judges, nor the power to enquire into their misbehaviour for 
malpractices or corruption. Article 124 (4) of the Constitution provides for the removal of a 
Judge only on the ground of proved misbehav iour or incapacity. The process of 
impeachment is cumbersome. Thus, introduction of effective alternative measures has become 
inescapable because of the constitutionally-assigned role of Supreme Court/High Court for 
protection of the fundamental rights of the people and ensuring justice to the citizens against 
draconian laws. The Commission, an institution so stregetic and transparent, must be 
manned by persons of proven integrity and unalloyed honesty beyond any external 
influence. One alternative could be that appointment of its Members be done by a 
Committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Minister of Law and Jusitce, the Speaker of 
Lok Sabha and the Leaders of the Opposition in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The panel 
of names for the appointment of Judges out of which Commission would finally appoint new 
Judges should have the approval of a Committee comprising Chief Justice of Supreme Court 
and Chief Justices of two High Courts identified by Chief Justice of India on a yearly 
rotational basis. 
Demand for compensation under Crop Insurance Scheme in 
Tamil Nadu 
SHRIR. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to put forward here the present 
gloomy condition of farmers in Thanjavur, Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam districts, who 
are continuously affected because of loss in agriculture for the last four years. They 
are seeking immediate alternative remedy such as provision of compensation under 
the Crop Insurance Scheme, which I had raised before in this august House. 
According to the present norms, the Insurance Corporation considers harvest for three 
consecutive years to calculate the average threshold yield of the present year for the 
provision of compensation to the affected farmers. But, unfortunately, for the last three years 
continuously, farmers of our area have been suffering continuous loss in agriculture. 
For example, for the last three years, our Tiruvarur District has been declared as drought-
affected district, and for the years 2001-2002, 2002-2003, and 2003-2004, insurance 
was declared as 5 per cent, 52 per cent and 47 per cent respectively, as in the year 2001-
2002, our areas were affected 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
due to adverse flood and during the next two years, by drought. Now, the insurance 
companies, as they did before, have followed the same method of considering the average 
threshold yield of three earlier years. 2001-2002,2002-2003 and 2003-2004 have been 
calculated to find out the actual percentage of loss occurred in the year 2004-2005. If the 
average yield is calculated for the three previous years which are drought years, the affected 
farmers cannot get the exact compensation. Hence, I request the Government to 
direct the concerned authority to calculate average loss of the present year taking into 
consideration the yield often years as special case instead of three years to save the affected 
farmers.

Demand to ensure quality check of petroleum products 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, petroleum products like petrol and diesel are 
supplied to public through retail outlets owned by the Government and private sector. 
For every consumer product, there is a provision for quality check. For checking the 
quality of milk supplied by the Government, co-operative and other agencies, there is 
lactometer. Even the quality of food served in restaurants is checked by the Health 
Inspectors. Even for woollen garments, there is a woolmark and for golden ornaments, there 
is hallmark. But, in the case of petroleum products, there is no provision for quality 
and quantity checks. 
There is a rampant adulteration of petroleum products like petrol and diesel throughout 
the country and especially in Tamil Nadu. Due to poor quality and adulteration of petrol 
and diesel, the pollution level has increased. Already, there is high level of vehicular 
pollution in major cities and this has increased. Sir, since adulterated petrol and diesel is 
being used, the engines of the vehicles are damaged earlier than their life term. Now-a-days, 
every household has a vehicle, and, therefore, all sections of the society are facing the 
problems. Moreover the health of the general public is also affected due to emissions from 
vehicles using adulterated fuel. 
I urge upon the Central Government to introduce a mechanism to check the quality of petrol 
and diesel supplied to the public through retail outlets. 
238 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In fact, I demand the Government to introduce legislation to check the quality of fuel just 
as in the case of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Adulteration would prove dangerous 
as fuel is also used by the airlines, railways, etc. I suggest that a meter should be kept in 
every retail outlet whether owned by the Government or a private owner so that the public 
can know the quality of fuel used in their vehicles.

Demand for retaining the present age limit for Civil Services 
Examination 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the Indian Administrative 
Service is an important and the highest civil service in the country. These officers are crucial 
for the implementation of policies and programmes of Governments both of State and Central 
level. The selection process for these categories is entrusted to the highest commission of 
the Central Government with specific eligibility, criteria and guidelines. 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
There are reports in the section of newspapers that the Government is going to lower the 
age limit for the candidates appearing for the Indian Administrative Service. Definitely, this 
will adversely affect those candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, 
Adivasis and OBCs. It will be a disadvantageous decision for these candidates belonging to 
rural and poorer sections since they are not in a position to compete with the rich 
candidates. 
The Constitution guarantees certain special provisions for these categories and the 
decision will infringe upon their rights. Many candidates belonging to these categories are 
agitated. 
Hence I request the Government not to reduce the age limit for candidates appearing for the 
India Administrative Service.
